title: Chirality inversion in DNA-assembled nanorod superlattices via site-specific asymmetric anchoring of single nanospheres
source: Physical sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Two-dimensional (2D) chiral superlattices of plasmonic nanoparticles have attracted considerable interest due to their broad potential across various fields. However, achieving facile control over their handedness without compromising structural integrity remains a persistent challenge. Here, we report a distinct class of 2D superlattices, 4-arm pinwheel arrays with tunable configurations, through defined patch size mismatch in DNA origami-templated assembly. A superlattice framework possessing preconfigured mirror-image units is created and utilized as a platform for DNA programming of chirality. We demonstrate a single-degree-of-freedom strategy that controls the handedness of the entire superlattice through DNA-enabled site-selective and asymmetric binding of a single gold nanoparticle into the mirror-image units. These local minimal perturbations preserve long-range crystalline order while generating opposite chiroptical responses via altered plasmonic near-field coupling. Our work expands the design scope of programmable materials toward chiral functional metasurfaces, and establishes a chirality-engineering approach that circumvents global structural reconstruction.

title: Sublevel-selective electron spin hyperpolarization of triplet radical pairs in metal–organic frameworks
source: Physical sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Molecular spin systems are promising platforms for spin-based technologies because their electronic structures can be synthetically tailored and integrated into higher-order assemblies. Photogenerated radical pairs can exhibit spin hyperpolarization under ambient conditions, yet extending such spin dynamics from isolated molecules to structurally organized materials remains challenging. Here, we report a metal–organic framework that regulates the generation of spin-polarized radical pairs within locally well-defined donor–acceptor arrangements. N,N’-di(4-pyridyl)−1,4,5,8-naphthalenetetracarboxdiimide is introduced into a zinc tetrakis(4-carboxyphenyl)porphyrin-based framework. Dense donor–acceptor packing promotes efficient quenching of the porphyrin singlet excited state and selectively forms strongly coupled triplet radical pairs polarized in the zero-spin projection sublevel. These radical pairs exhibit narrow electron paramagnetic resonance signals and long spin-lattice relaxation times. Their spin-lattice relaxation dynamics persist in various guest solvents and vary with guest identity, demonstrating a route to chemically responsive spin materials based on porous, locally organized donor–acceptor frameworks.

title: Room-temperature continuous-wave lasing-like emission from solution-processed bulk monolayer MoS2 thin films
source: Physical sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) are promising laser-gain media for their direct bandgap and strong excitonic effects. However, existing TMD lasers typically rely on mechanically exfoliated or high-temperature chemical-vapor-deposition-grown materials, with their atomic-scale thickness inherently limiting the available optical gain volume. Here, we report room-temperature continuous-wave lasing-like emission from solution-processed bulk monolayer MoS2 (BM-MoS2) thin films in whispering-gallery-mode (WGM) cavities. Using solution exfoliation and spray coating under ambient conditions, we produce area- and thickness-scalable BM-MoS2 films composed of electronically decoupled MoS2 monolayers separated by organic spacers. This layered architecture preserves the intrinsic monolayer excitonic properties while providing a tunable gain volume beyond that of an isolated monolayer. Integrated with WGM cavities, the thickness-scalable BM-MoS2 films enable a balance between the quality (Q) and optical confinement (\(\varGamma\)) factors. Power-dependent measurements reveal key lasing signatures, including a threshold-like input-output crossover accompanied by linewidth narrowing at a pump power of approximately 1.4 nW, and pump-induced polarization selection. Solution-processable BM-MoS2 thus offers a scalable gain medium for thin-film laser photonics.

title: Dynamic chlorine vacancies enable X-ray-specific afterglow
source: Physical sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Afterglow luminescence in inorganic materials is conventionally attributed to pre-existing static defects that trap and gradually release charge carriers. However, the observation of afterglow activated only by specific types of excitation sources, such as X-ray-specific afterglow in certain phosphors, highlights an opportunity to move beyond this static trap model. Here we show that Bi3+ doped Cs2ZrCl6 crystals exhibit afterglow exclusively under X-ray excitation, with no such effect under ultraviolet illumination. We demonstrate that this behavior arises from the in-situ generation and self-healing of metastable chlorine vacancies (VCl) specifically driven by X-ray irradiation, directly correlating with afterglow kinetics. Advancing beyond previous vague attributions to Frenkel defects, our multimodal evidence unambiguously pinpoints VCl as the operative defect species. This discovery challenges the paradigm that afterglow requires static pre-existing traps, establishing a dynamic mechanism where metastable defects are created by the probing radiation and gradually disappear when radiation is removed. We further manipulate the afterglow kinetic through Sn4+ induced modulation of vacancy formation energy, extending the afterglow duration to multiple hours while maintaining a high light yield of 55670 photons MeV−1 and a low detection limit of 30.81 nGyair s−1. Finally, we integrate these crystals into a flexible PDMS composite film for X-ray imaging, achieving a high spatial resolution of 23.6 lp mm−1 that enables high-fidelity imaging of curved objects via time-resolved readout. Our findings open an avenue for designing smart scintillators with programmable, radiation-specific responses, with implications for flexible radiography and beyond.

title: Thermodynamic-guided tailoring of single-atom coordination environments via oxygen chemical potential for efficient C-N coupling
source: Physical sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Systematic and precise regulation of coordination environments in single-atom catalysts (SACs) remains challenging due to thermodynamic constraints and kinetic traps. Herein, we report a thermodynamic-guided strategy to tailor the local coordination of Fe single atoms on CoWO4 support by regulating oxygen chemical potential. Via fine-tuning hydrogen partial pressure during pyrolysis, a series of Fe1Ox SACs is synthesized with well-defined Fe-O coordination numbers ranging from 3 to 6. Combining operando characterizations and density functional theory calculations, Fe1O4 is identified as the optimal configuration for hexamethylenetetramine (HMTA) electrosynthesis, which delivers balanced kinetics by moderating free water dissociation for *NH3 generation and strengthening HCHO chemisorption via pronounced Fe 3d-O 2p orbital hybridization near the Fermi level. As a result, the Fe1O4 SAC achieves a HMTA yield of 0.21 mmol h−1 cm−2 with 83.04% Faradaic efficiency at 1.75 V and stability over 200 h in a flow cell. This work establishes a universal thermodynamic approach for precise coordination engineering of single-atom electrocatalysts and provides a general paradigm for kinetically balancing complex multi-intermediate electrocatalytic systems.

title: Depth-enhanced molecular imaging with two-photon oblique plane microscopy
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: High-numerical-aperture (NA) oblique plane microscopy enables noninvasive fluorescence imaging of subcellular dynamics without radical sample modification. However, performance degrades at depth in multicellular specimens as scattering and refractive-index heterogeneity raise out-of-focus background. We report a two-photon oblique plane microscope that improves resolution at depth by combining high-NA single-objective detection with multiphoton plane illumination. The microscope achieves ~ 300 nm lateral and ~ 650 nm axial resolution, with single-molecule sensitivity and 5 × faster volumetric acquisition (up to 3.25 × 106 voxels s−1). In multicellular contexts, near-infrared nonlinear excitation enhances contrast throughout the illumination depth by ~ 2 × and restores volumetric resolving power by > 2 × relative to linear excitation. We demonstrate these capabilities through molecular imaging of epithelial tissue, stem-cell-derived gastruloids, and living fruit fly embryos, including multicolor transcription-factor dynamics, optogenetic subcellular control, and single-mRNA tracking, all using standard glass-based mounting.

title: Energy poverty in an era of geopolitical instability: The role of Chinese FDI and south–south cooperation in Africa
source: ScienceDirect Publication: Energy Policy
abstract: The rising geopolitical fragmentation, driven by geopolitical tensions, conflicts and wars, has reshaped the global energy landscape, increasing uncertainty and vulnerability in energy markets. These disruptions present serious challenges for different economies in the Global South, where countries already face significant difficulties in facilitating energy transition and mitigating energy poverty. In this context, South-South cooperation may represent an important tool to address energy challenges, particularly through foreign investment. This study investigates the contribution of Chinese FDI to reducing energy poverty in Africa through different channels and whether conflict conditions influence the extent to which Chinese FDI contributes to improving energy outcomes. Our study contributes to the literature on the role of Chinese foreign capital in reducing energy poverty in Africa by examining both the underlying mechanisms and the potential role of conflict conditions in shaping these effects. To empirically explore this complex nexus, we rely on Structural Equation Modelling using a set of energy and socioeconomic variables from 2005 to 2022. The findings reveal a significant positive association between Chinese FDI and energy performance, with the prosperity channel representing the main mechanism. This association appears weaker in conflict-affected contexts, suggesting that geopolitical stability conditions the extent to which foreign investment is associated with improved energy outcomes. Policymakers in the region should consider creating a more attractive and stable investment environment to promote trade ties with Chinese companies, as these ties could be used as a tool to alleviate energy poverty.

title: The heterogeneous transmission of geopolitical energy shocks: A structural framework
source: ScienceDirect Publication: Energy Policy

title: Triarm Polycaprolactone Interface for Spatially Controlled Functionalization of Carbon Nanotube Fibers
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Carbon nanotube fibers (CNTF) with exceptional strength, electrical, and thermal conductivities possess the potential for deployment in electrochemical and analytical applications. For such applications, CNTF are typically encapsulated using polymeric interface membranes such as polyvinyl chloride (PVC) for accommodating functional elements or recognition molecules. These membranes typically assemble stochastically on CNTF surfaces owing to the nonuniform interfacial interaction energies between the characteristic groups of the polymers and the CNTF surface. This stochastic assembly of encapsulating membranes subsequently inhibits the homogeneous distribution of recognition molecules on the CNTF surface, which influences the analytical performances. Herein, a triarm polycaprolactone (3-PCL) block copolymer is designed to homogenize the interfacial energies between the polymeric membranes and the CNTF surface. The 3-PCL interface is hypothesized to enable spatially controlled assembly of polymeric membranes on the CNTF surface and subsequently a homogeneous distribution of recognition molecules. As an illustration, the CNTF with a 3-PCL interface is demonstrated as an ion-selective microelectrode (ISE) for selective and sensitive detection of ammonium ions (NH4+) via homogeneous incorporation of a NH4+-specific ionophores within an encapsulating PVC membrane on the CNTF surface. An LOD and linear response range of 1 × 10–7 M and 1 × 10–7 to 1.0 × 10–1 M, respectively, were achieved. These values are an order higher as compared to ionophores incorporated within the PVC membrane on the CNTF surface without the 3-PCL interface. Further, a linear two-arm polymer (2-PCL) was evaluated as an interface for validation of significantly higher and stable analytical responses that could be achieved using the 3-PCL interface. Thus, the 3-PCL possesses the potential to be an ideal interface for incorporation of functional materials and recognition elements within polymeric membranes on the CNTF surface for the development of high-performance electrochemical and analytical devices.

title: The emerging geopolitics of sustainable aviation fuel: Policy architectures, book-and-claim and european strategic dependencies
source: ScienceDirect Publication: Energy Policy
abstract: Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) is becoming a strategic component of aviation decarbonization, but its expansion depends on technological, economic, institutional, and resource conditions. This study compares the combinations of policy instruments, structural production characteristics, and market-governance arrangements observed in the European Union, the United States, the United Kingdom, Japan, Singapore, and Brazil, and considers the potential strategic vulnerabilities these configurations suggest, particularly for the European Union. The comparative qualitative policy analysis draws on peer-reviewed literature, legislation, regulatory documents, and institutional sources, organized through a single four-part framework: policy-instrument mix; structural production conditions; market and governance conditions; and potential strategic vulnerabilities. The cases display different configurations. The European Union and the United Kingdom emphasize mandatory demand; the United States relies more heavily on producer incentives; Japan and Singapore emphasize coordination and supply security; and Brazil combines established biofuel capabilities with a developing SAF framework. These observations do not identify causal effects or rank the configurations. Instead, they indicate possible exposure to feedstock, production, finance, policy-continuity, import, and certification constraints. Book-and-Claim is examined as a governance arrangement that separates environmental attributes from physical fuel flows; its practical contribution depends on credible certification, verification, registry governance, and interoperability. For the European Union, the comparison suggests that regulatory leadership may coexist with external supply and institutional dependencies. The concept of resilient interdependence is therefore proposed as a policy lens rather than a measured outcome.

title: Is inclusive green growth resilient to energy-related geopolitical risk? The role of energy affordability as a binding constraint
source: ScienceDirect Publication: Energy Policy

title: Physical distancing to prevent influenza-like illness on a college campus: The eX-FLU trial
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Public health recommendations often advise people to isolate when infected with influenza-like illness (ILI) with the goal of promoting physical distancing and limiting face-to-face interactions when risk of transmission is highest. Because isolation may have negative consequences, it is important to carefully assess whether encouragement to physically distance actually prevents cases of ILI. College campuses can be especially vulnerable to outbreaks of ILI and are ideal environments for assessing the impact of encouragement-to-physically-distance interventions. The eX-FLU cluster-randomized trial followed 579 students on a college campus over a ten-week period during flu season to evaluate such an intervention. Students in the trial were randomized to receive the intervention—encouragement to isolate in their dorm room when symptomatic for ILI—or control. Evaluating the effect of this intervention is challenging because of dependence between students in the trial and an anticipated spillover effect of the intervention. Moreover, while the intervention was designed to affect both face-to-face interactions and ILI infections, the effect on ILI infections is of primary public health interest. In this paper, a randomization-based testing procedure is proposed to assess the intervention effect specifically on ILI infections in the presence of dependent data and spillover effects. The testing procedure is shown theoretically and empirically to control the type I error rate and have good statistical power to detect an intervention effect in trials similar to eX-FLU. When applied to the eX-FLU data, this testing procedure gives moderate evidence that the intervention reduced ILI infections.

title: An LHX2-DACH1 regulatory innovation drives basal progenitor expansion in the primate neocortex
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: A defining feature of the primate neocortex is an expanded cortical progenitor pool, especially the basal radial glia (bRG), contributing to complex intracortical circuitry underlying higher cognition. Here, a comparative transcriptomic analysis of developing human and mouse neocortical cells identified DACH1 as a transcription factor enriched in human neurogenic RGs. Using both primate ESCs and mouse models, we found an LHX2-DACH1-miR-215-5p program regulating bRG production. DACH1 loss in human cortical progenitors impaired bRG production and shifted neuronal output toward corticospinal neurons, whereas Dach1 depletion in mice had no effect. Conversely, ectopic DACH1 expression in the rodent neocortex induced bRG formation and promoted callosal neuron production. Further, we found that DACH1 is regulated by LHX2 via a primate-evolved enhancer. Introducing this enhancer into mice promoted bRG generation, while its removal in primates impaired bRG production. Mechanistically, DACH1 promotes bRG generation by suppressing miR-215-5p–mediated down-regulation of centromere- and centrosome-related genes. These findings reveal a mechanism by which cortical progenitor expansion shapes the primate cortical connectome for cognitive evolution.

title: Increases in Northern Hemisphere winter circulation waviness over 1989 to 2011 driven by decadal oceanic variability
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Large-scale circulation waviness shapes day-to-day weather and extremes. During 1989 to 2011, Northern Hemisphere midlatitudes experienced a pronounced increase in wintertime waviness, coinciding with rapid Arctic warming and more frequent cold-air outbreaks. While Arctic amplification was hypothesized to cause this trend via jet weakening, subsequent studies have failed to support this mechanism, leaving the origin unresolved. Here, using large-ensemble simulations, statistical analyses, and dynamical diagnostics, we demonstrate that variability in sea surface temperature and sea ice accounts for approximately half (48.7 to 63.3%) of the observed increase. A positive phase shift of the Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation (AMO) is the prominent driver, enhancing waviness across northern Eurasia, the northwest Pacific, and the North Atlantic. A concurrent negative Interdecadal Pacific Oscillation shift partially offsets the AMO-driven anomalies in the northwest Pacific. Projections indicate that internal variability will outweigh model differences as the main source of near-term uncertainty. These results refine attribution of recent winter waviness changes and identify an AMO-linked source of predictability for long-term shifts in midlatitude extremes.

title: Time-evolved hetero-alkali interphases enable long-life sulfide-based anode-free solid-state batteries
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Sulfide-based anode-free solid-state batteries (AFSSBs) offer high energy density and improved safety, but their practical implementation is hindered by parasitic reactions between freshly plated lithium (Li) and sulfide solid electrolytes. These reactions continuously consume the limited cathode-derived Li inventory, increase interfacial impedance, and promote nonuniform Li plating and stripping. Here, sodium bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide (NaFSI) is incorporated into Li 5.4 PS 4.4 Cl 1.6 (LPSC) to kinetically program interphase evolution. Heat treatment initially generates a NaF/LiF-rich interphase on the LPSC surface. This fluoride-rich region chemically stabilizes the interface and suppresses direct LPSC reduction. During the early cycles, the outermost region progressively evolves into a LiF/Li 3 N-rich layer, while the NaF-containing phase becomes buried beneath the Li-rich surface region, producing a time-evolved compositional gradient. Although NaF provides effective chemical passivation, its poor Li + conductivity can impede interfacial ion transport. The subsequent formation of Li 3 N-rich domains, which exhibit substantially higher Li + conductivity than NaF, provides more favorable transport pathways, homogenizes interfacial Li + flux, and promotes uniform Li plating and stripping. This time-evolved gradient interphase therefore combines early-stage chemical stabilization and Li conservation with improved long-term ion transport kinetics, suppressing impedance growth, localized inactive Li accumulation, and filamentary shorting. Consequently, the AFSSB using the NaFSI-modified LPSC interlayer retains 77.6% of its capacity after 500 cycles at 0.2 C, whereas the cell with bare LPSC retains only 32.1% after 100 cycles. These findings establish temporally programmed gradient interphases as a general strategy for conserving active Li and stabilizing sulfide-based AFSSBs.

title: Origins of low density and low accretion rate in classical T Tauri stars
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: High-resolution x-ray spectroscopy of classical T Tauri stars (CTTs) reveals a soft x-ray excess, low electron density, and accretion rate inferred from helium-like oxygen (O VII). Accretion shock models have been widely studied via numerical simulations and can reproduce observations with appropriate accretion stream structures. Within the standard accretion shock framework, we propose a distinct physical model involving energy exchange between postshock hot plasma and cold infalling material during reverse shock propagation into the accretion stream. Incorporating charge exchange processes, the electron density derived from the O VII triplet shows excellent agreement with helium-like neon diagnostics and standard accretion shock model predictions. The mass accretion rate inferred from O VII emission also becomes consistent with optical results. Complementing our theoretical work, we conducted a laboratory simulation of CTT accretion shocks supported by hydrodynamic similarity principles. Time-integrated x-ray self-emission and temporal optical shadowgraphy reveal the dynamic formation of two dense clumps, the “core” and “shell,” which morphologically resemble hydrodynamic oscillations driven by heating/cooling instabilities in CTT accretion shocks. The core is a standing shock formed by a preheated low-density plasma flow impinging on a carbon-hydrogen foil, while the shell is shocked aluminum plasma (the reverse shock) arising from interactions between accumulated aluminum plasma and its following flow. High-resolution experimental spectra confirm that charge exchange occurs in the shocked x-ray–emitting region. Our results demonstrate that dynamic interactions between postshock and infalling material, mediated by charge exchange cooling, is the reason for the low O VII density problem in CTTs.

title: Dynamical geometric modes in non-Euclidean plates
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Continuum elastic shells with residual stresses can exhibit complex motions that require vanishing elastic energy to excite, also called geometric zero modes, enabling them to be driven by weak and generic energy inputs. Despite recent interest in these modes, we understand very little about their dynamical properties. Plates with a curved, rather than flat, in-plane geometry, also called non-Euclidean plates, are one example in which residual stresses and geometry combine to produce a continuum of ground states. The plate can explore these states through a geometric zero mode when it has the shape of a minimal surface—a surface with zero mean curvature. We demonstrate that a non-Euclidean plate with the shape of a saddle minimal surface exhibits the predicted continuous stability, but this degeneracy is ultimately lifted by aging. Despite developing a preferred configuration, the zero mode remains the softest mode. Using a combination of analytical theory and experiments, we show that the elastodynamics of this soft mode is captured by the dynamics of a damped pendulum. A periodic driving uncovers resonance phenomena in this pendulum mode, such as small oscillations and steady rotations, but mixes with an additional flapping mode at high frequencies.

title: Identification of gamma-hydroxybutyrate (GHB)–β-ribose as a promising biomarker enabling prolonged detection of GHB intake
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: For several years, forensic toxicologists have sought biomarkers to extend the detection window of gamma-hydroxybutyric acid (GHB), a drug suspected to be involved in drug-facilitated sexual assaults yet difficult to detect due to its rapid elimination, endogenous presence, and postsampling formation. In this study, we used samples from 30 participants in a double-blind, controlled trial, randomized to placebo or a single oral dose (50 milligrams per kilogram) of sodium oxybate, a GHB salt. We collected whole blood and urine samples over 5 days and used untargeted metabolomics to search for biomarkers. The most promising feature, previously suggested as a GHB-pentose, was identified as GHB-β-ribose by chemical synthesis and liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry. Quantification showed elevated levels of GHB-β-ribose for up to 48 in blood and 24 hours in urine after GHB intake compared with endogenous levels in the placebo group and authentic forensic cases. Thus, we present GHB-β-ribose as a very promising biomarker for GHB intake, with the potential to extend the detection window for GHB.

title: Structural and biochemical insight into allosteric regulation of the human 2-aminoadipic semialdehyde synthase
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Multiple clinically relevant inborn errors of metabolism occur in lysine degradation, yet the regulation of this biochemical pathway remains poorly understood. The initial rate-limiting step of lysine catabolism is catalyzed by the bifunctional enzyme 2-aminoadipic semialdehyde synthase (AASS). Here, we report the cryo-EM structure of the full-length 400-kilodalton tetrameric AASS enzyme complex with substrates and products bound to both the lysine-2-oxoglutarate (LOR) and saccharopine dehydrogenase (SDH) catalytic domains. We also identified allosteric compounds that modulate the activity of AASS by reacting with cysteine-414 and shifting the pH optimum for biochemical activity. The mutagenesis of this allosteric Cys 414 has marked effects on the enzyme’s conformation and activity despite being more than 12 angstrom from the active site. We find that small changes near the hinge of an enzyme can have large effects on its catalytic properties. Last, targeting allosteric cysteines may be a general strategy for modulating enzyme activity by altering the dynamics of the enzyme.

title: Lynx1 suppression reopens the window for effective rehabilitation after stroke in mice
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Rehabilitation is an effective and reliable approach for promoting motor recovery after stroke. However, its efficacy decreases during the transition from the subacute to the chronic phase after stroke, posing a major barrier to complete functional recovery. This limited efficacy during the chronic phase is believed to result from declining neural plasticity. However, the molecular and cellular mechanisms regulating neural plasticity and its temporal changes after stroke remain unclear. To address this gap, we established a focal ischemic stroke mouse model that allows causal interrogation of the mechanisms responsible for the reduced efficacy of rehabilitation in the chronic phase. Using this model, we identified Lynx1, an endogenous negative allosteric modulator of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, as a negative regulator of post-stroke neural plasticity. Lynx1 expression in layer 5 pyramidal neurons was transiently down-regulated and returned to normal levels in the peri-infarct area. Longitudinal intravital imaging revealed that Lynx1 suppression promoted synaptic clustering with increased dendritic spine turnover in the peri-infarct area, an emerging structural basis for memory formation. As anticipated, Lynx1 suppression improved spontaneous motor recovery and the efficacy of rehabilitation in the chronic phase after stroke. Furthermore, we developed a Lynx1 -targeting antisense oligonucleotide and found that its administration during the chronic phase after stroke enhanced the efficacy of rehabilitation. These findings suggest that dendritic spine dynamics in the peri-infarct area are a key determinant of rehabilitation responsiveness through the regulation of clustered spine formation and that Lynx1 may represent a promising therapeutic target for augmenting dendritic plasticity after stroke.

title: Selectively disrupting lysine acetyltransferase p300 and ZEB1 interaction prevents tumor progression while enhancing antitumor immunity
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Both p300 acetyltransferase inhibitors and bromodomain inhibitors show therapeutic promise in cancer, but they mostly exhibit limited efficacy and may elicit severe adverse effects due to their lack of targeting selectivity. Thus, selectively disrupting p300 interactions with specific pro-oncogenic targets that are specifically expressed in neoplastic cells could serve as a safe and effective strategy for cancer treatment. Here, we demonstrate that p300 interacts with the pro-oncogenic transcription factor, ZEB1, and catalyzes its acetylation at an evolutionarily conserved K80 residue, stabilizing its expression in aggressive cancer cells. Ectopic expression of wild-type ZEB1 (mostly in acetylated status) but not the acetylation-deficient ZEB1 mutant modulates cytokinome of cancer cells, creating an immune-suppressive tumor microenvironment to support cancer progression. Underlining the importance of ZEB1 posttranslational processing, the K80-acetylated transcription factor is highly expressed in human cancers where its high-level expression is associated with poor prognosis. Importantly, we identify a small molecule compound, WY6, that undergoes high-affinity binding to p300 TAZ2 domain (a domain critical for ZEB1 binding) and consequently disrupts ZEB1 binding to p300, thereby suppressing K80 acetylation. WY6 treatment of tumor cells effectively represses p300-mediated ZEB1 acetylation, promoting its ubiquitination and subsequent degradation. Moreover, in vivo, WY6 potently suppresses orthotopic tumor growth without eliciting obvious toxic side effects and exhibits a synergetic effect when combined with PD-1/PD-L1 blockade immunotherapy. Collectively, our data demonstrate that selective disrupting of p300 and ZEB1 interaction effectively prevents tumor progression and may offer a promising therapeutic strategy for p300–ZEB1 axis-driven malignancies.

title: Elastic interactions of mechanically polarizable cells
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Cells mechanically interact through the deformations they generate in their surrounding extracellular matrix. We present an analytical theory of the elastic interactions between cells that actively adapt their forces in response to local deformations of their environment. Cells are represented as localized contractile force generators, modeled as polarizable point force dipoles, whose adaptive forces are determined self-consistently with those of surrounding cells. Analysis of the associated elastic interaction energy identifies a generic short-ranged interaction arising from the mutual adaptation of cellular forces. This induced-dipole interaction is analogous to the van der Waals interaction between molecules and likewise is shown to be generally attractive for cells that enhance contractility in response to stretch. Furthermore, unlike the long-ranged elastic interaction between nonpolarizable force-dipoles, that peaks at intermediate matrix stiffness and then weakens as the matrix softens, the induced-dipole interaction strengthens monotonically as the matrix softens and can reverse the interaction from being repulsive at long cell distances to being attractive at short separations. Analytical calculations are presented to illustrate the mutual polarization of forces in pairs of interacting cells on a substrate. The identification of a generic, short-range cohesive elastic interaction between cells is important for understanding cell behavior at short separations and provides a physical mechanism driving cell accumulation on soft substrates.

title: Two-phase NEUROD1 pioneer activity synchronizes sensory neuronal differentiation and subtype specification
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Temporal control of neuronal differentiation is essential for establishing stable neuronal identities, yet the transcriptional and epigenetic mechanisms underlying this process remain poorly understood. Using auditory neurons as an in vivo model, we investigate the role of the proneural factor NEUROD1 in regulating neuronal differentiation timing and subtype specification. To bypass early neuronal loss in germline
                    Neurod1
                    deletion mutants, we generated a delayed, self-terminating conditional knockout mouse (
                    Neurod1ST
                    ) that permits analysis of later differentiation stages. Integration of NEUROD1 chromatin binding and histone profiling at embryonic day (E) 11.5 with transcriptomic analyses across E11.5, E14.5, and E18.5 reveals a two-phase regulatory program during auditory neuron development that parallels dynamic
                    Neurod1
                    expression. In the first phase, coinciding with
                    Neurod1
                    upregulation during early neuronal differentiation, NEUROD1 preferentially binds putative enhancers of neuronal differentiation genes and promotes their transition to active chromatin states, consistent with pioneer factor activity. Loss of
                    Neurod1
                    disrupts these epigenomic transitions, resulting in persistence of progenitor-like states with premature activation of differentiation and axonogenesis programs. This dysregulation is accompanied by activation of alternative regulatory networks, leading to defective neuronal migration and innervation, progressive identity instability, and apoptosis. In the second phase, marked by reexpression of
                    Neurod1
                    in developing Type Ib/Ic precursors,
                    Neurod1
                    deletion selectively impairs Type Ic specification while promoting a Type Ib-like identity. These findings identify NEUROD1 as a temporal regulator that coordinates developmental progression and stabilizes auditory neuron identity through phased regulatory activity, providing a mechanistic framework for how pioneer transcription factors couple chromatin remodeling to developmental timing.

title: The developmental semantic–temporal relation extends beyond discrete sense representations
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query

title: An end-to-end machine-learning system for global eddy-resolving ocean forecast
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Machine learning (ML) models, especially those based on deep neural networks, have achieved competitive forecast accuracy and greatly reduced computational burden compared to traditional numerical global ocean forecast systems (GOFSs). However, it remains difficult for these ML models to operate on their own, as they rely on the initial conditions generated by numerical GOFSs. In this study, we present WenHai-E2E, an end-to-end ML GOFS that replaces the entire pipeline of numerical GOFSs at deployment time and makes eddy-resolving global ocean forecast directly from multisource heterogeneous ocean observations, without requiring operational initial conditions from numerical GOFSs. WenHai-E2E outperforms a state-of-the-art numerical GOFS in the forecast accuracy. Our results demonstrate the promise of ML GOFSs to surpass numerical GOFSs and provide insight into the pathway for developing next generation of GOFSs.

title: People know who to ask for favors despite underestimating compliance
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Whether and how people approach social interactions hinges on how they expect others to respond. Extensive social psychology research suggests that people are inaccurate interpersonal perceivers, overestimating negative responses (e.g., discomfort) and underestimating positive responses (e.g., appreciation) across a variety of social situations. However, this conclusion is based almost exclusively on mean-level bias analyses that obscure the dyadic nature of interpersonal judgment and rely on a narrow conceptualization of interpersonal accuracy. Leveraging research on favor-asking and anticipated compliance as an exemplar, we demonstrate that interpersonal accuracy takes multiple theoretically distinct forms, and that the prevailing conclusion that people misunderstand their influence over others—because they tend to underestimate compliance—is likely overgeneralized. Across four studies (13,196 directed dyadic ratings), we show that people accurately differentiate between
                    who
                    will comply with
                    their
                    favor requests (dyadic meta-accuracy) despite the average tendency to underestimate compliance (mean-level bias). This pattern emerged for specific and general favor requests, among well- and newly-acquainted individuals, and beyond what could be expected due to self-projection. Through this dyadic lens, people are highly adept judges of their influence over others, as they are able to target their requests toward individuals who are uniquely likely to acquiesce to them—and can avoid wasting time on those who are not. Thus, our research refines existing implications for how people approach asking for favors. More broadly, by aligning theory, measurement, and level of analysis, our studies elucidate the need for greater theoretical precision and empirical breadth in interpersonal accuracy research.

title: Raising mountains for a habitable Earth
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: The formation of mountain belts (orogens) elevates rocks above sea level, making them available for chemical weathering and altering the composition of the atmosphere and oceans, which in turn control habitability. Peak-metamorphic pressures recorded by crustal rocks buried in orogens increased between 2.7 to 2.2 and 0.8 to 0.7 billion years ago, indicating that rocks could be buried deeper and that orogens could grow substantially thicker after each of these periods. The two periods of orogenic growth were broadly synchronous with major increases in terrigenous element and nutrient fluxes and changes in biological sulfur metabolism and surface oxygenation. These changes could be explained by enhanced weathering of higher mountains. The findings support the hypothesis that there are first-order mechanistic links between secular geodynamic change and changes in Earth system state and habitability, which shaped the conditions for the evolution of complex life during the past 3 billion years.

title: Emergent long-tailed dynamics in spin ice
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: In this study, we reveal long-tail dynamics spontaneously arising from a magnetic system. Specifically, we consider a classical spin system and demonstrate the emergence of a spin-ice physics when drive-induced heating is well suppressed. We show that at high driving frequencies, magnetic monopole excitations exhibit nonergodic stochastic dynamics characterized by power-law-distributed trapping times with long tails—a behavior that persists even in the absence of driving. At intermediate driving frequencies, the system eventually heats up to an infinite-temperature state. However, contrary to conventional wisdom of Floquet heating, the heating time in our model is extremely sensitive to different initial-state realizations and also follows a long-tailed power-law distribution, which arise specifically due to periodic driving. We show that an effective short-range attractive interaction between monopoles is responsible for the long-tailed distributions observed in both monopole and heating dynamics.
