title: An inspiral of a star inside a common envelope with its giant companion
source: Nature
abstract: The formation of compact stellar binaries requires rapid orbital tightening of their progenitor binary stars1,2. This is theorized to happen through common envelope evolution (CEE)3, when the stars orbit in a loosely bound, shared convective envelope, triggering an inspiral due to frictional drag4,5. However, this inspiral in such a system has never been observed directly. Here we present observations of AT 2025abao, a transient eruption in the Andromeda Galaxy, which originates from the CEE of an approximately 7M⊙ asymptotic giant branch (AGB) star with its companion. Extensive pre- and post-eruption spectroscopy is best explained as an approximately 0.7M⊙ companion inspiralling within the convective AGB envelope that powers a seven-year period of gradual brighteningone of the first direct observations of frictional drag energy dissipation induced by CEE. This phase is radiatively efficient, consistent with predictions for convective transport in CEE5, 6, 7–8. The subsequent merger of the companion with the primary core powers the ejection of the outermost 10% of the stellar envelope at speeds about 10× the primary escape speed, and empirically constrains the fraction of dissipated orbital energy available to unbind the convective common envelope4,9, 10–11, 0.01 ≲ α ≲ 0.4. This end-to-end characterization using multi-survey observations demonstrates a path towards mapping the landscape of CEE outcomes with upcoming surveys. Observations of AT 2025abao provide direct evidence of common-envelope inspiral, revealing frictional energy dissipation and constraining how orbital energy drives stellar-envelope ejection during binary evolution.

title: Hypothalamic volume and cell-type changes in ageing and Alzheimer’s disease
source: Nature
abstract: Alterations in metabolism, stress response, sleep, circadian rhythms and neuroendocrine processes are key features of ageing and neurodegeneration1,2. These fundamental processes are regulated by the hypothalamus, yet how its functionally distinct subregions and cell types change during human ageing and Alzheimer's disease (AD) remains largely unexplored. Here we present HypoAD, an atlas of the human hypothalamus in ageing and AD, including high-resolution magnetic resonance imaging from 458 individuals and single-nucleus RNA sequencing of 614,403 nuclei from young participants, patients with AD and age-matched non-dementia control participants. We show that hypothalamic subregions governing metabolism, stress and circadian rhythms are particularly vulnerable, showing notable changes in both volumes and gene expression during ageing and AD. At the molecular level, machine learning models identified the inflammatory response and regulators of circadian rhythms as key cellular predictors of AD. These signatures were reflected in specific cell types: microglia transitioned to a pro-inflammatory state, whereas inhibitory neurons within sleep-regulating and circadian-regulating hypothalamic subregions showed the most profound transcriptional alterations, including disruptions in ligand-receptor interactions and G-protein-coupled receptor signalling. HypoAD provides a high-resolution volumetric map and a transcriptomic atlas of the human hypothalamus in ageing and AD, relating lifestyle and behavioural changes to the relevant volumetric and molecular pathways. In addition, HypoAD provides a framework to investigate hypothalamic dysfunction and establishes a roadmap for targeted interventions aimed at mitigating physiological disruptions to potentially slow disease progression.

title: Tropical land-use intensification restructures biodiversity
source: Nature
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Tropical land-use intensification threatens global biodiversity, yet most assessments of tropical agricultural landscapes focus on local-scale biodiversity, overlooking how land use restructures biodiversity across space and multiple taxa. Here we provide an ecosystem-wide assessment of 24 taxonomic groups across all domains of life—encompassing 40,049 species—along a land-use intensification gradient from lowland forests to intensively managed smallholder cash-crop monocultures in Indonesian landscapes. Despite widespread losses of landscape and local multidiversity
                    1
                    in monocultures (approximately 78% and 50%, respectively), we found no evidence for consistent community homogenization with land-use intensification. Instead, monocultures exhibit a systematic shift from turnover to nestedness for aboveground taxa. Such patterns of differentiation may mask trajectories towards biotic homogenization via early stages of assemblage simplification. Biotic differentiation has the potential to partly mitigate biodiversity losses by positively affecting γ-diversity. This opens management options, including the conservation of existing remnants of traditional agriculture and the implementation of sustainable management practices
                    2–4
                    . Our results demonstrate that tropical land-use intensification restructures biodiversity not only through species loss, but also via a pervasive reorganization of community composition across trophic levels. Conserving tropical biodiversity, therefore, requires a multi-taxon, landscape-scale perspective that explicitly integrates agricultural land uses with the protection of natural and semi-natural habitats to reconcile agricultural production and conservation.

title: Transient contacts between filaments impart its elasticity to branched actin
source: Nature
abstract: Cells dynamically assemble actin into branched networks to push on their environment during cell migration, endocytosis or the maintenance of cell-cell contact1. These networks are among the stiffest found in the cytoskeleton and can generate large pushing stresses against stationary obstacles2-5. When grown against a controlled opposing stress in an atomic force microscope6 or inside the cell7, branched networks alter their own architecture to adapt their compressional stiffness to their environment, but the underpinnings of their mechanics and adaptability are unclear. Here we show that their high density and low connectivity place them outside the scope of standard elastic network models for actin. We show that they are instead dominated by the proliferation of interfilament contacts under compression. This places branched actin in the same category as undercoordinated fibrous materials such as sheep's wool. When the network is grown under force, filaments entangle as if knitted together and trap contacts in their structure. Trapped contacts have a similar role as crosslinkers in rigidifying the network and are thus key to its active adaptive mechanics.

title: Band-Edge-Extended Heterointerfaces for Perovskite Solar Cells and Tandems
source: Nature
abstract: Perovskite solar cells (PSCs) have emerged as a promising photovoltaic technology, with efficiencies rapidly approaching those of established crystalline-silicon solar cells. Further efficiency gains, however, are increasingly limited by charge extraction and recombination at the interface between the perovskite absorber and the electron-transport layer. Interfacial modifiers are widely used to suppress these losses, yet many conventional ammonium-based modifiers are weakly electronically coupled to the perovskite surface and can introduce barriers to electron extraction 1-5. Here we realize electronically coupled heterointerfaces by introducing a family of heteroatom-containing, fully conjugated formamidinium interfacial modulators, establishing band-edge-extending conjugated heterointerfaces that overcome the bottleneck of inefficient interfacial electron transfer. The resulting band-edge-extended heterointerface establishes delocalized electron connectivity at the perovskite/electron transporting layer (ETL) interface and suppresses interfacial non-radiative recombination. We report a certified power-conversion efficiency (PCE) of 27.96% and a stabilized power output (SPO) of 27.84% for inverted PSCs. The corresponding devices retained over 95% of their initial efficiency after 2000 h continuous maximum-power-point tracking under 1-sun irradiation (ISOS-L). Extending this strategy to monolithic perovskite–silicon tandems enables a certified SPO of 34.71%, establishing band-edge extension as a broadly applicable approach to overcoming the conventional trade-off between interfacial passivation and charge extraction.

title: Designing dislocation-driven polar vortex networks in twisted perovskites
source: Nature
abstract: Twisting two atomic layers produces a geometric moiré pattern but bonding-induced interfacial reconstruction fundamentally transforms this into an ordered dislocation network-a distinction obscured in weakly bonded van der Waals systems. Although in-plane topological vortex nanostructures arising from twisting-induced lateral strain modulation have been linked to periodic moiré patterns in freestanding perovskite layers1-3 and 2D bilayers4, their coupling to the interfacial dislocation network in twisted layers remains unresolved. Here we demonstrate that twisted freestanding SrTiO3 (STO) layers undergo interfacial reconstruction into a network of screw dislocations, accompanied by the emergence of in-plane topological vortices. Unlike in previous reports, these vortices are associated with the dislocation network rather than with geometric moiré patterns. Four-dimensional scanning transmission electron microscopy (4DSTEM) reveals a beam deflection texture in registry with the interfacial dislocation network. A machine learning interatomic potential, trained on first-principles calculations, together with phase-field modelling, confirms that competing strains within the dislocation network stabilize polar vortex-antivortex pairs; first-principles calculations further reveal the emergence of an electronic superlattice with a well-defined periodicity. Our results establish twist-controlled dislocation networks as a new and versatile route to designing local polar and electronic structures in oxide materials.

title: Closest relatives of poxviruses prevail in human and animal guts worldwide
source: Nature
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Large and giant double-stranded DNA viruses substantially affect eukaryotic ecology and evolution
                    1–4
                    . They prevail in the environment but are rarely found in the digestive system of animals
                    5,6
                    . Here we present the discovery of a diversified group of DNA viruses with large linear genomes, dubbed egoviruses, that comprise a putative viral order most closely related to animal-infecting poxviruses. Egoviruses are found worldwide, almost exclusively in the digestive system of humans, livestock and wild animals. The most prevalent human-specific egovirus is spread across continents, demonstrating a long-term association between egoviruses and the human gut microbiome. Eukaryotic homologues of egovirus core genes suggest that these viruses primarily infect Trichostomatia (ciliates), which assist ruminant digestive processes
                    7
                    , and Parabasalia (Metamonada), which influence animal immunity and gut microbiome ecology
                    8
                    . Egoviruses also contributed to the genetic makeup of polintons, endogenous viruses that proliferated in genomes of
                    Trichomonas
                    vaginalis
                    9
                    and its close Parabasalia relatives. Unlike poxviruses that form brick-shaped virions, egoviruses are predicted to form multilayered icosahedral capsids resembling those of asfuviruses and probably representing the ancestral virion structure. Egoviruses are the only known clade of double-stranded DNA viruses of eukaryotes prevailing in the animal digestive system. Phylogenomic analysis suggests an evolutionary scenario whereby egovirus-like ancestors of poxviruses infected anaerobic unicellular eukaryotes inside the gut of ancestral animals, before transitioning to animal cell infection, which was accompanied by the virion metamorphosis.

title: Evidence for late Middle Pleistocene Homo erectus in mainland East Asia
source: Nature
abstract: Hominin fossils and genetic evidence indicate that several hominin populations occupied East and Southeast Asia during the Middle and Late Pleistocene epoch1-10. Homo erectus fossils remain scarce in southern China and mainland Southeast Asia4,8,11. Here we report nine newly discovered late Middle Pleistocene hominin teeth from the Naxian and Baxian caves at the Chongzuo study area, Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, southern China, dated to around 324-184 thousand years ago12. Palaeoproteomics reveals the presence of an endogenous dental proteome in all five hominin teeth studied molecularly. Four teeth contain a derived H. erectus substitution in ameloblastin that to date has been observed only in older Middle Pleistocene H. erectus specimens from China13. The proteomes of these four teeth differ from the previous H. erectus proteomes from China at another ameloblastin position, suggesting that these specimens represent a previously unsampled H. erectus population. Morphometric and geometric morphometric methods support an attribution of these teeth to H. erectus, as well as four additional teeth. This fills a gap in the geographical and chronological distribution of H. erectus in East Asia. The fifth tooth studied proteomically, PA1796, is morphologically distinct from H. erectus, Neanderthals (Homo neanderthalensis) and modern humans (Homo sapiens), and does not contain the H. erectus-derived amino acid sequence. The late survival of H. erectus on mainland East Asia suggests that at least two hominin lineages, H. erectus and Homo longi (Denisovans)6,7, possibly represented by PA1796, were present in the region towards the end of the Middle Pleistocene, with the first documented occurrence of H. sapiens not much later5.

title: Structural and regulatory evolution across the genus Hordeum
source: Nature
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    The genus
                    Hordeum
                    comprises cultivated barley and its wild relatives, an evolutionarily, ecologically and agriculturally important group of grasses
                    1,2
                    . Here we generated a chromosome-scale comparative genomic resource comprising all recognized diploid
                    Hordeum
                    species together with representative polyploid lineages. Comparative analyses reveal extensive structural variation, including inversions and chromosomal rearrangements that disrupt proximal collinearity and reflect lineage-specific genome remodelling. Single-copy gene phylogenies identify ancient hybridization, segmental exchange and introgression, revealing pervasive reticulate evolution during
                    Hordeum
                    diversification. We uncover widespread horizontal gene transfer from Panicoideae grasses into
                    Hordeum
                    , with many transferred genes showing evidence of transcription and functional integration. Retrotransposon proliferation explains genome size variation and provides insights into polyploid genome evolution. Whole-genome alignments reveal contrasting evolutionary dynamics: whereas coding sequences remain highly conserved, regulatory elements undergo rapid turnover, providing a rich source of regulatory diversity for phenotypic evolution. Case studies of vernalization and glume development demonstrate how natural variation in regulatory and coding sequences contributes to flowering time and floral morphology. This comprehensive pangenomic framework establishes
                    Hordeum
                    as a model for studying genome evolution, structural variation and the genetic basis of adaptive traits, offering new avenues for barley improvement.

title: Injury-induced signalling coordinates immunity and cannibalism in locusts
source: Nature
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Cannibalism, the consumption of conspecifics, is widespread across the animal kingdom and can profoundly influence individual fitness and population dynamics
                    1,2
                    . Although the ecological and social conditions that favour cannibalism have been well documented
                    2
                    , the molecular signals that trigger cannibalistic attacks have remained poorly understood. Here we show that in
                    Locusta migratoria
                    , guaiacol, a volatile compound with augmented release after injury, attracts gregarious nymphs and induces cannibalistic behaviour. Guaiacol is detected by olfactory receptors LmOR36 and LmOR34, and disruption of either receptor abolishes attraction, thereby impairing induction of cannibalism. Guaiacol is synthesized by haemolymph symbiont
                    Enterobacter hormaechei
                    . Injury promotes bacterial congregation at the wound site, leading to elevated guaiacol production through a clustered set of vanillic acid decarboxylase genes; deletion of this gene cluster abolishes guaiacol production and its behavioural effects. Notably, guaiacol initially functions as a beneficial signal after injury. Guaiacol activates immune-related pathways in wounded locusts, enhancing pathogen resistance and increasing survival following minor injury. However, when guaiacol emission exceeds a threshold determined by injury severity, it functions as an external cue that attracts cannibals. Cannibalistic locusts exploit this immune-related odour to locate severely injured conspecifics, gaining both nutritional resources and immune system benefits. Together, our findings identify a microbial–chemical mechanism that links immune defence with cannibalistic behaviour and provide potential molecular targets for manipulation of cannibalism-dependent population dynamics.

title: High-Throughput Screening of Photocatalytic Metal–Organic Frameworks for CO2 Reduction Using Relational Data Extraction and Hierarchical Machine Learning
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Photocatalytic carbon dioxide reduction (CO2RR) over metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) is governed by both framework features and reaction conditions, which complicate catalyst discovery and render general design rules difficult to establish. In this study, we develop a synergistic machine-learning workflow to integrate literature data extraction, electronic-property prediction, and hierarchical classification for prioritizing MOF photocatalysts. First, a literature-derived record-level data set containing catalyst compositions, structural descriptors, reaction conditions, and catalytic outcomes was curated through large language model (LLM)-assisted relation extraction followed by manual verification. Then, a transfer-learning crystal graph convolutional neural network (CGCNN) model was trained for band gap prediction at the Heyd-Scuseria-Ernzerhof screened hybrid functional (HSE06) level, achieving a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.31 eV against reference HSE06 calculations. Subsequently, a physically constrained multitask framework was employed to predict electron affinity (EA) and ionization potential (IP) for thermodynamic prescreening. Three record-level classifiers were constructed for activity screening (C1), performance classification (C2), and product selectivity prediction (C3). When applied to the Computation-Ready, Experimental (CoRE) MOF database under standardized gas- and liquid-phase inference settings, the workflow prioritized 639 primary candidates, with most assigned to CO formation. Probability calibration and applicability-domain analysis further identified 166 of these candidates (25.98%) as a more stringent calibrated, in-domain subset. Overall, this study provides a practical data-driven workflow for condition-resolved prioritization of MOF photocatalysts and analysis of descriptor-level trends associated with photocatalytic CO2RR.

title: Ferroptosis in cancer cells triggers PGE2 production for tumour immune escape
source: Nature
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Ferroptosis, a form of cell death induced by overwhelming membrane lipid peroxidation, is a vulnerability of many cancers, including cancers resistant to current molecular and immune-based therapies
                    1–7
                    . Triggering of ferroptosis therefore provides an opportunity to achieve elimination of difficult-to-treat cancers
                    1–4,8,9
                    . Studies in mouse cancer models have demonstrated that anticancer immunity, mediated by dendritic cells (DCs) and CD8
                    +
                    T cells, is essential for effective tumour eradication by ferroptosis-inducing strategies
                    10–13
                    . However, ferroptotic cells limit this response
                    8–10,14
                    , resulting in immune escape and tumour growth through mechanisms that remain unclear. Here we demonstrate that ferroptotic cancer cells activate a molecular program resulting in aberrant production of prostaglandin E
                    2
                    (PGE
                    2
                    ), which limits the stimulation of anticancer CD8
                    +
                    T cell responses by type 1 conventional DCs (cDC1s), thereby promoting immune escape. In ferroptotic cancer cells, lipid peroxidation-mediated membrane permeabilization enables Ca
                    2+
                    influx, which activates p38 MAPK signalling and thereby drives PGE
                    2
                    production. This signalling axis is uncoupled from cancer cell death and can be targeted to selectively interfere with immune-inhibitory PGE
                    2
                    production while preserving ferroptotic cancer cell elimination. In the context of cancer cell ferroptosis, ablation of PGE
                    2
                    production or disrupting PGE
                    2
                    signalling restores cDC1-mediated anticancer CD8
                    +
                    T cell responses and leads to effective tumour elimination. Our findings identify a key mechanism that limits antitumour immunity and prevents tumour elimination upon ferroptosis induction in cancer cells, which could be exploited for cancer therapy.

The discovery of such viruses that prevail in the digestive system of humans and animals exposes a long-overlooked facet of the gut microbiome that clarifies the origin of poxviruses.

title: Evidence for p-wave magnetism in electronic band structure of metallic EuSi
source: Nature
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    One active frontier of quantum-matter research is the realization of
                    p
                    -wave symmetry-breaking phases in fermionic systems, long exemplified by the A phase of superfluid helium-3 (refs.
                    1–3
                    ). Achieving
                    p
                    -wave superconductivity
                    4
                    and its magnetic analogue
                    5
                    —characterized by a time-reversal-symmetric,
                    p
                    -wave spin-polarized Fermi surface—remains a grand challenge
                    6,7
                    . Despite recent progress in identifying candidate
                    p
                    -wave magnets
                    5,7–10
                    , spin-resolved spectroscopic evidence for their electronic structures remains limited. Here we report angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) and spin-ARPES evidence for
                    p
                    -wave magnetism in the near-Fermi-level electronic structure of stoichiometric metallic EuSi, supported by symmetry analysis, first-principles calculations and neutron scattering. Neutron diffraction reveals a chiral spiral phase between 33.4 K and 62 K that fulfils archetypal
                    p
                    -wave magnetism criteria: it preserves the combined symmetry of time reversal and lattice translation, while breaking inversion symmetry. Spin-integrated ARPES reveals a pronounced magnetism-driven reconstruction of the electronic structure, with energy separations exceeding 100 meV, and spin-ARPES resolves
                    S
                    
                      y
                    
                    polarization in near-Fermi-level spectral features. The extracted
                    S
                    
                      y
                    
                    exhibits a sign-changing modulation across successive magnetic Brillouin zones and is suppressed near the nodal regions, consistent with the predicted
                    p
                    -wave spin texture and unfolded spin-polarization calculations. Magnetic force microscopy and micro-ARPES further reveal approximately 10-μm chiral magnetic domains. These results identify EuSi as a stoichiometric metallic platform for investigating
                    p
                    -wave magnetism in electronic band structures and spin-symmetry-based functionalities in spintronics
                    10
                    , topological matter
                    7
                    , superconductivity
                    11
                    and beyond.

title: Halogen‐Dependent Regulation of the Thyroid Hormone Transporter by Antipsychotic Drugs and Their Analogues
source: Angewandte Chemie International Edition
abstract: ABSTRACT Antipsychotic drugs are primarily used to manage psychosis and other psychotic disorders. Their main mechanism of action involves blocking dopamine D2 receptors in the brain, and they remain important for the treatment for schizophrenia. In this paper, we describe an unusual property of several commonly used antipsychotic drugs and their analogues for their ability to modulate the thyroid hormone transporter system. Specifically, these compounds significantly increase the protein expression of monocarboxylate transporter 8 (MCT8), a key transporter responsible for carrying thyroid hormones across the plasma membrane in a variety of cell lines. Our findings indicate that the presence of halogen substituents plays a critical role in promoting the MCT8 upregulation. Furthermore, the magnitude of this effect is dependent on the nature of the halogen atom, with iodine‐containing phenothiazine derivatives exhibiting the strongest induction of MCT8 expression. The increased transporter expression was accompanied by enhanced cellular uptake of MCT8‐selective fluorescent probes, confirming functional activity. To the best of our knowledge, this study provides the first example of halogen‐dependent regulation of protein expression in mammalian cells.

title: Resolving Ultrafast Electronic and Chiral Structural Dynamics That Govern Circularly Polarized Luminescence from Eu(III) Antenna Complexes
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Circularly polarized luminescence (CPL) from chiral molecules and materials has promising applications in display technology, optical sensing, and quantum information science. However, luminescent-state configurations that approach the maximum degree of circular polarization in emission have only been achieved in exceptional cases, most notably in Eu(III) antenna complexes. An open challenge is the understanding and suppression of detrimental relaxation dynamics of the CPL-active state, which can distort carefully designed ground-state configurations and quench luminescence. We now resolve these processes for the prototypical Eu(III) antenna complex CsEu((+,−)-hfbc)4 (hfbc = 3-heptafluorobutyrylcamphorate) by mapping its complete electronic and chiral structural evolution with ultrafast circular dichroism spectroscopy. Combined with transient absorption measurements and electronic structure calculations, we unravel the intramolecular energy transfer from the helically arranged antenna ligands to the emissive metal ion, and extract the stereochemical configuration of all involved excited states through their ligand-centered circular dichroism. We find that population transfer proceeds from delocalized singlet excitonic states via a ligand-localized triplet, while a parallel singlet exciton trapping channel unexpectedly quenches luminescence. Remarkably, excitation of the luminescent Eu(III) ion increases the helical twist of the ligand sphere by 2.7 ± 1.3° toward an ideal square-antiprismatic geometry, where the CPL performance is most favorable. The excited 4f-orbitals thus drive non-negligible changes in the primary coordination sphere, challenging common assumptions in 4f coordination chemistry and elucidating the need for ligand antenna rigidification to maximize the CPL performance of Ln(III)-based emitters. This work establishes a general framework to unravel the ultrafast excited-state dynamics governing CPL emission.

title: Intracellular Bacterial Imprinting Enables Preservable Whole‐Cell Vaccination
source: Wiley: Advanced Materials: Table of Contents
abstract: ABSTRACT Whole‐tumor‐cell vaccines preserve broad tumor‐antigen repertoires, but converting living tumor cells into safe and intrinsically immunogenic vaccine substrates remains challenging. Here we generated bacteria‐imprinted tumor (BiT) cells through the controlled internalization of attenuated Salmonella and subsequently prepared them as nonproliferative cellular vaccines by freeze‐drying. Within a defined bacterial‐loading window, intracellular Salmonella induced endoplasmic reticulum stress‐associated immunogenic preprogramming while preserving tumor‐cell integrity, thereby enhancing danger‐signal exposure, antigen‐presentation capacity, and immune visibility. Freeze‐drying preserved the bacteria‐induced immunogenic imprint by retaining key molecular and functional attributes while maintaining overall cellular architecture and markedly reducing residual bacterial viability. Vaccination with freeze‐dried BiT (FD‐BiT) cells elicited coordinated innate and adaptive immune responses, including antigen‐presenting cell activation, T follicular helper‐B‐cell cooperation, and germinal‐center formation. This coordinated T–B cell response was accompanied by durable memory formation and enhanced intratumoral CD8 + T‐cell infiltration, proliferation, and functional maintenance. Accordingly, FD‐BiT reduced primary tumor establishment and pulmonary metastasis and restrained the growth of tumors that emerged despite prophylactic vaccination. These findings establish intracellular bacterial programming and freeze‐drying‐mediated imprint preservation as a cell‐engineering principle for whole‐tumor‐cell vaccination.

title: Single-atom catalyst–Li2O2 interfacial chemistry governs the activity–stability trade-off in Li–O2 batteries
source: National Science Review Advance Access
abstract: Cathode catalysts in aprotic Li–O2 batteries are commonly judged by their ability to lower charge overpotentials, yet improved catalytic activity often does not lead to durable cycling. Here, we use structurally well-defined M–N4 single-atom catalysts (SACs) as model cathodes to elucidate the interplay between catalyst activity and battery stability. Integrated experimental and theoretical studies suggest that, although SACs promote Li2O2 oxidation and lower the initial charging overpotential, they also increase the reactivity of discharge-generated Li2O2 toward ether electrolytes, promoting carboxylate accumulation and cathode passivation. On the basis of this mechanistic insight, a localized high-concentration electrolyte is introduced to regulate the catalyst–Li2O2 interfacial chemistry, suppress side reactions, and extend the cycling life from 42 to 398 cycles. This work identifies a previously overlooked trade-off between catalytic activity and battery stability in Li–O2 batteries and provides a mechanistic foundation for designing stable catalyst/electrolyte interfaces in high-energy electrochemical devices.

title: Reactive Phase Conversion‐Enabled 1D/3D Heterostructure Engineering Toward High‐Performance Perovskite Photovoltaics
source: Wiley: Advanced Materials: Table of Contents
abstract: ABSTRACT We report a reactive phase conversion strategy for 1D/3D heterostructure engineering in perovskite photovoltaics. During crystallization, 1‐carboxymethyl‐3‐methylimidazolium chloride (CMMIMCl) reacts with PbI 2 , enabling the in situ formation of one‐dimensional (1D) CMMIMPbI 3 within the 3D perovskite matrix. This precursor‐level process simultaneously consumes residual PbI 2 and constructs an internally coupled 1D/3D heterostructure, which regulates crystallization kinetics, promotes oriented crystal growth, and redistributes residual stress. The resulting 1D framework further modulates defect energetics and interfacial charge transport, thereby suppressing non‐radiative recombination and ion migration. Notably, at an optimized low CMMIMCl concentration, the initially formed 1D‐related species potentially serve as crystallization templates, modifying the crystallization pathway and facilitating more complete conversion of PbI 2 into high‐quality 3D perovskite. Benefiting from these integrated structural and optoelectronic improvements, inverted perovskite solar cells (PSCs) achieve a champion power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 27.09% (certified 26.98%), while scalable perovskite modules reach 22.01%. Furthermore, wide‐bandgap PSCs achieve a PCE of 23.66%, enabling perovskite/tunnel oxide passivated contact tandem devices with an efficiency of 33.03% (certified 32.98%). This work establishes a versatile route for simultaneous regulation of crystallization, defects, strain, and charge transport in high‐performance perovskite photovoltaics.

title: Acoustic‐Electromagnetic Information Sensing and Security Protection via Intelligent Transparency Metasurfaces
source: Advanced Materials
abstract: ABSTRACT Acoustic‐electromagnetic (EM) cross‐domain sensing converts information carried by sound‐induced mechanical vibrations into remotely measurable EM signals, supporting applications in human–computer interaction, environmental sensing, and the Internet of Things. However, the ability to reconstruct acoustic information from weak phase signatures in EM echoes also creates a risk of acoustic information leakage. Existing shielding and encryption schemes are difficult to combine with covert integration and real‐time reconfigurability, and struggle to intervene directly in the mapping process, thereby are poorly suited to end‐to‐end threats in complex scenarios. Here, we propose an interface for cross‐domain sensing and security protection based on an optically transparent intelligent metasurface with reconfigurable control over echo amplitude and phase. The intelligent metasurface reshapes the acoustic‐to‐EM mapping and controls the demodulated output without altering the acoustic source signal. We fabricate a prototype with programmable amplitude and phase control and partial optical transparency. Experiments demonstrate three controllable effects along the acoustic–EM transduction chain: acoustic information suppression, ambiguity generation, and hallucinatory speech output in the absence of acoustic excitation. This work provides an integrable and configurable physical‐layer paradigm for cross‐domain protection and information manipulation in cross‐domain sensing systems.

title: Enhancing the Photocatalytic CO 2 Reduction of Spinel Co Sites Under an Alternating Magnetic Field by Regulating Their Spin State
source: Wiley: Advanced Materials: Table of Contents
abstract: ABSTRACT The integration of spin‐engineered catalysts with an external alternating magnetic field (AMF) in a collaborative manner has emerged as an appealing approach to enhancing photocatalytic performance. However, the intrinsic correlation between spin state of catalyst and the magnetic field‐assisted mechanism still needs to be explored. Here, we propose a spin‐state modulation strategy involving the selective substitution of the geometric configuration of Co sites in the NiCo 2 O 4 /C 3 N 4 heterojunction. Separately incorporating Zn and Cr atoms into tetrahedral and octahedral sites induces a charge redistribution that converts low‐spin Co 3+ sites into intermediate‐ and high‐spin states, respectively. Detailed characterizations and theoretical simulations reveal that an AMF can increase the concentration of CO 2 ‐derived intermediates on the surface of the spin‐engineered catalysts. This enhancement is strongly correlated with the spin configuration of Co sites. The modulated arrangement of electrons in cobalt alters the corresponding d‐band center under AMF, consequently optimizing the binding strength of crucial intermediates. Remarkably, the Zn‐doped sample with an intermediate‐spin state exhibits an impressive CO production rate of 318.3 µmol g – 1 h −1 under an AMF, which is 15 times higher than without AMF assistance. This work provides new insight into developing efficient spin‐related catalysts with the help of an external magnetic field.

title: In Situ Programming of Armored CAR‐Macrophages by Microneedle‐Mediated Gene Delivery for Melanoma Immunotherapy
source: Wiley: Advanced Materials: Table of Contents
abstract: ABSTRACT Despite clinical advances in CAR‐T therapy and immune checkpoint blockade, effective immunotherapy for solid tumors remains limited by restricted immune‐cell access and an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. Chimeric antigen receptor macrophages (CAR‐M) provide an alternative strategy by combining antigen‐directed myeloid programming with local immune remodeling. A self‐locking microneedle platform incorporating mannose‐modified nanoparticles (MNPs) enables localized in situ programming of CAR‐expressing macrophages at melanoma sites. The platform co‐delivers a tumor‐antigen‐directed CAR and a hypoxia‐responsive anti‐PD‐L1 single‐chain variable fragment (scPD‐L1). Initial studies in B16F10‐OVA tumors establish antigen‐dependent CAR activity and coordinated local immune remodeling. Therapeutic efficacy is subsequently evaluated in parental B16F10 tumors using an endogenous tyrosinase‐related protein 1 (TYRP1)‐directed CAR. MNP(TYRP1/scPD‐L1) microneedles delay tumor progression, prolong survival, and promote coordinated myeloid and CD8 + T‐cell responses, while providing lower terminal tumor burden, greater local surface CAR + tumor‐associated macrophage abundance, and reduced systemic exposure compared with dose‐matched intratumoral administration. Reciprocal depletion further shows that CAR‐programmed macrophages contribute to the antigen‐directed myeloid response, whereas CD8 + T cells are major downstream effectors required for maximal and sustained tumor control. These findings establish a localized transcutaneous strategy that coordinates antigen‐directed myeloid programming with adaptive antitumor immunity.

title: Biomimetic Subcellular Chemomechanical Nano‐Regulator for Allergic Rhinitis Treatment
source: Wiley: Advanced Materials: Table of Contents
abstract: ABSTRACT Allergic rhinitis (AR) is a highly prevalent and debilitating chronic inflammatory disease; however, its complex pathophysiological mechanisms remain incompletely explored, resulting in a significant lack of effective therapeutic strategies in clinical practice. Here, we found that the submucosal extracellular matrix undergoes profound pathological stiffening during AR development and is associated with severe epithelial mechanometabolic dysfunction and physical barrier collapse. Based on this pathomechanical observation, we developed a spatiotemporally programmable subcellular chemomechanical regulator (SCM) to reconstruct the damaged mucosal barrier. Capitalizing on its precise targeting and cascade‐responsive capabilities, SCM provides immediate anti‐inflammatory activity to stabilize stressed epithelial cells. Beyond this acute intervention, the regulator scavenges intracellular free radicals, attenuates pathological mitochondria‐associated membrane (MAM) over‐coupling, and restores mitochondrial metabolic homeostasis. In parallel, the Mn‐containing nanocore and pirfenidone jointly attenuate fibroblast activation and abnormal extracellular‐matrix stiffening. Formulation‐resolved cellular and animal studies distinguished a predominant TA‐associated contribution to early inflammatory and epithelial‐barrier responses from a predominant PFD‐associated contribution to later matrix remodeling. Full SCM combined these stage‐associated response domains while rebuilding epithelial‐barrier integrity and shifting systemic immune readouts toward tolerance. These findings provide a preclinical mechanobiology‐guided framework for treating AR and other mechanically driven inflammatory diseases.

title: Oxygen Anchoring Enabled by Ce‐Based Pyrochlore Coating for Robust Lithium‐Ion Battery Cathodes
source: Wiley: Advanced Materials: Table of Contents
abstract: ABSTRACT Nickel‐rich layered oxides (≥ 80% Ni) are pivotal cathode materials for next‐generation high‐energy lithium‐ion batteries. However, under high cutoff voltage, the over‐oxidation of active cations and oxygen anions triggers structural instability and the continuous migration of O n− (0 n 0.84 Co 0.08 Mn 0.08 O 2 (NCM) during cycling. Combining a Ce‐based pyrochlore coating that possesses a high oxygen storage capacity with bulk Ce doping that modulates the TM─O bonds, the modified NCM cathode exhibits exceptional cycling stability under harsh operating conditions. The assembled CR2032 cells achieved 72.2% capacity retention after 400 cycles at 1 C under a high cutoff voltage of 4.50 V at 60°C. Moreover, pouch‐type full cells exhibit ultra‐stable cycling performance, retaining 91.0% capacity after 1000 cycles at 1 C within 2.75–4.20 V, and 80.2% after 1000 cycles when the upper cutoff voltage is raised to 4.40 V. This work not only provides a feasible two‐pronged modification strategy for layered oxide cathodes but also promotes the development of ultrahigh‐energy‐density rechargeable batteries.

title: Stage‐Specific Pressure Programming Decouples Low‐Pressure Sulfur Reduction From High‐Pressure Interfacial Reconstruction in All‐Solid‐State Lithium–Sulfur Batteries
source: Wiley: Advanced Materials: Table of Contents
abstract: ABSTRACT The commercialization of all‐solid‐state Li–S batteries (ASSLSBs) remains constrained by the “impossible trinity” between high energy density, long cycle life, and low stack pressure. Here we show that stack pressure is not merely a static mechanical boundary, but a stage‐specific regulator of sulfur conversion and interfacial reconstruction. Using a static pressure‐resistance‐overpotential (P‐R‐η) operational threshold algorithm, low‐stack‐pressure operation is predicted feasible for 50 wt% S cathodes. Further operando electrochemical measurements and multiscale chemical and structural characterizations reveal that 1 MPa discharge promotes Li 2 S 2 ‐rich interfacial intermediates. However, constant low‐pressure cycling induces progressive pore filling that prolongs charge transport pathways, leading to inactive Li X S accumulation and triphase interfacial contact losses. State‐resolved very‐small‐angle neutron scattering (VSANS) further uncovers a ∼5 nm structural feature that persists after low‐stack‐pressure discharge, which specifically diminishes upon high‐pressure charging. Guided by this mechanism, we implement a pressure‐programmed protocol combining 1 MPa discharge with 180 MPa charge. The resulting cell retains 98.8% of capacity after 100 cycles at 30 °C. This work establishes a dynamic pressure modulation strategy towards alleviating the “impossible trinity” by decoupling the asymmetric pressure‐electrochemical behaviors.

title: Microstructure Engineering of Organic Mixed Ionic‐Electronic Conductors, an Emerging Toolbox for Performance Enhancement and New Applications
source: Wiley: Advanced Materials: Table of Contents
abstract: ABSTRACT Organic mixed ionic‐electronic conductors (OMIECs) have attracted growing attention for biointegrated electronics and human‐robot interfaces because they can transduce ionic signals into electronic outputs, while offering mechanical compliance for seamless integration with soft biological systems. Achieving high‐performance in OMIEC‐based devices requires precise control over structural parameters across multiple length scales, from molecular‐level chemical structure to macroscopic device architecture. Particularly, because OMIECs operate through direct contact with electrolytes and rely on coupled ionic and electronic transport, microstructural engineering provides a powerful strategy to regulate the electrolyte‐OMIEC interface, ion‐transport pathways, and volumetric doping behavior, thereby bridging molecular design and device‐level architecture. In this review, we categorize microstructural engineering strategies for OMIECs across different length scales, ranging from nanoscale phase‐separated domains to microscale porous and three‐dimensional architectures, and discuss the underlying structure‐formation mechanisms and key processing parameters of each approach. Using organic electrochemical transistors (OECTs) as a benchmark platform, we summarize how these strategies have been implemented to enhance device performance and enable new functionalities, while also highlighting their limitations and remaining challenges. Finally, we examine applications of microstructured OMIECs beyond OECTs, focusing on electrochromic devices, and discuss future directions for establishing a deeper understanding of microstructure‐property relationships in mixed ionic‐electronic conducting materials.

title: Precursor–Cavity Compatibility Directs C−N Bond Evolution Toward Edge Reconstruction for H 2 O 2 Electrosynthesis
source: Wiley: Advanced Materials: Table of Contents
abstract: ABSTRACT ZIF‐derived metal–nitrogen–carbon (M−N−C) catalysts provide a versatile platform for constructing atomically dispersed metal sites, yet their pyrolysis‐driven local coordination evolution remains largely governed by stochastic reconstruction processes. The lack of predictive structural descriptors linking molecular precursors with atomic‐scale active‐site evolution limits the rational design of high‐performance M−N−C catalysts. Here, we identify precursor–cavity compatibility as a key geometric descriptor that steers confined pyrolysis pathways and regulates C−N bond cleavage, leading to the formation of defect‐rich, edge‐reconstructed Co−N 4 environments. The optimized Co(bpy) 3 ‐NC achieves 95.9% H 2 O 2 selectivity at 0.60 V versus RHE and sustains nearly 90% Faradaic efficiency for 120 h at 200 mA cm −2 in an ambient‐air‐fed flow cell. Mechanistic investigations reveal that the reconstructed Co−N 4 environments optimize Co−OOH interaction by balancing *OOH stabilization with O−O bond preservation, thereby favoring the selective 2e − ORR pathway. Furthermore, the electrogenerated dilute H 2 O 2 stream enables effective nitrite regulation in recirculating aquaculture systems, demonstrating the potential of integrating molecularly guided catalyst design with decentralized chemical production. This work establishes precursor–cavity compatibility as a rational design principle for steering atomic‐scale coordination evolution in confined pyrolysis.

title: Modulating Compound Orientations by Modular Synthesis of Lyotropic Liquid Crystalline Alignment Media
source: Wiley: Advanced Materials: Table of Contents
abstract: ABSTRACT The unambiguous determination of relative configuration is an indispensable part of modern compound development in chemistry and medicine. Anisotropic NMR parameters, like residual dipolar couplings (RDCs), are of global nature providing angular structure information and thus complement established structure elucidation methods. RDCs become accessible if the compound in question is oriented with respect to the magnetic field, for example, by using a lyotropic liquid crystal. Modern approaches of RDC‐based structure elucidation do not rely on a priori models of structure and dynamics but require RDC sets of several linearly independent orientations. Herein, the modular synthesis of a series of substituted polyglutamates, all of which form lyotropic liquid crystals in organic solvents, is presented. The new alignment media become accessible from a time‐efficient and straightforward procedure, additionally giving access to functionalities inaccessible via conventional polypeptide synthesis. The orientation of a model compound is investigated as a function of the different side chain motifs. It is demonstrated that these different side chain motifs are clustered into different categories, with linearly independent orientations provided across these clusters. We demonstrate that data are highly complementary, allowing structure elucidation of a model compound using vector orientations from 1 D C‐H ( 1 D C‐C for methyl groups) RDCs as only restraints.

title: Manipulating Monomicelle Monolayer Assembly via Salt Effect Toward Tailorable Mesoporous Polydopamine Superstructures for Aqueous Batteries
source: Wiley: Advanced Materials: Table of Contents
abstract: ABSTRACT The inherent thermodynamic instability of isotropic soft micelles drives their conventional bulk aggregation toward multilayered mesoporous structures, while stabilizing monomicelles and manipulating their monolayer assembly into mesoporous superstructures poses a significant challenge. Here, we report a salt effect‐modulated monomicelle assembly strategy for the precise construction of monolayer mesoporous polydopamine superstructures. The concerted salt effect arising from Debye screening and salting‐out stabilizes the composite monomicelles, reduces their hydrophilicity, and promotes their migration and lateral monolayer assembly at the emulsion interface. Increasing the salt content accelerates assembly kinetics, enhances interfacial affinity, and increases micellar rigidity, enabling tunable interfacial coverage and thereby producing a series of monolayer mesoporous superstructures, including monolayer honeycomb‐like mesoporous nanosheets, monolayer honeycomb‐like mesoporous vesicles, monolayer compound eye‐like mesoporous vesicles, and monolayer compound eye‐like mesoporous nanosheets. As a proof of concept, monolayer honeycomb‐like nanosheets with open mesochannels and abundant functional groups were demonstrated as a nano‐ion divider. By homogenizing the ion flux and enhancing ion affinity and transport, this architecture enables dendrite‐free Sn aqueous batteries with an exceptional lifespan of 2794 h. This work opens new avenues for constructing monolayer superstructures with unparalleled architectural modularization.

title: Probing Phonon Dynamics for Kinetic Stabilization of Single‐Crystal Nickel‐Rich Cathodes
source: Wiley: Advanced Materials: Table of Contents
abstract: ABSTRACT Structural degradation and lattice oxygen loss remain major obstacles to the long‐term stability of nickel‐rich layered cathodes, especially under high‐voltage and high‐rate operation. Conventional strategies primarily rely on thermodynamic stabilization via cation doping or surface protection, while the kinetic dimension of oxygen release has received less attention. Herein, we investigate Si─Ti co‐doped single‐crystal LiNi 0.83 Co 0.12 Mn 0.05 O 2 cathode materials, which exhibit reduced Li/Ni mixing, modified surface chemistry, and altered transition metal–oxygen (TM─O) lattice dynamics. Combined Raman spectroscopy and phonon dispersion calculations suggest that Si─Ti co‐doping enhances phonon scattering and modifies TM─O optical phonon modes. Operando and synchrotron‐based characterizations reveal substantially enhanced reversibility of lattice oxygen redox and transition‐metal local coordination. As a result, the optimized cathode exhibits suppressed oxygen release and mitigated irreversible phase transitions, retaining 83.17% of its initial capacity after 1000 cycles at 5 C. These improvements are likely associated with the synergistic effects of thermodynamic and kinetic stabilization, with phonon dynamics proposed as one possible contributor among these coupled effects. This work highlights that the kinetic factors relevant to oxygen release warrant greater attention in the design of durable Ni‐rich cathodes.

title: Brønsted Acid Enrichment Around Zeolite‐Encapsulated Pd Promotes Efficient Tandem Catalysis
source: Angewandte Chemie International Edition
abstract: ABSTRACT Metal‐acid bifunctional catalyst design is essential for selectivity control in tandem catalysis. However, reactive intermediates often experience a kinetic mismatch between metal‐ and acid‐catalyzed elementary steps, thereby being consumed through competing pathways and diverted toward undesired products. Herein, we developed a metal cation‐directed Al siting (MCD‐Al) strategy to enrich framework Al sites around Pd nanoparticles encapsulated in Beta zeolite (Pd@Beta‐MCD), enabling tunable Brønsted acid site density close to metal sites by controlling metal precursor loading. When Pd@Beta‐MCD was employed in benzene hydroalkylation, the spatial proximity of metal–acid sites accelerated transfer of Pd‐generated cyclohexene to adjacent acid sites, and the high Brønsted acid site density around Pd nanoparticles remarkably facilitated cyclohexene protonation for alkylation. Pd@Beta‐MCD achieved its maximum cyclohexylbenzene yield of 48.1% with a corresponding selectivity of 77.5%, outperforming Pd/HBeta (21.1% and 30.1%) and Pd@HBeta (27.7% and 38.3%), representing the best performance reported to date for this reaction. Moreover, Pd@Beta‐MCD showed superior cycling stability over eight runs. We demonstrated that the concentrated Brønsted acid sites adjacent to metal centers resolve the kinetic mismatch and steer the cyclohexene intermediate toward an alkylation‐dominated pathway. This work provides an effective strategy to strengthen metal–acid synergistic matching and facilitates precise control of key intermediates in tandem catalysis.

title: The effect of inorganic impurities in post-consumer plastic waste on the catalytic cracking of polyolefins
source: Nature Chemical Engineering
abstract: Polyolefin upcycling is challenged by inorganic impurities in post-consumer plastic waste. Here the authors show that common metal contaminants, particularly zeolite poisons such as Na, K, Ca, Mg and Cu, drive catalyst deactivation during cracking, while sulfur and chlorine are more benign. The catalyst remains active over extended operation and has the potential to yield cleaner pyrolysis oils than thermal pyrolysis.

title: Stepwise Alloying‐Driven Local Chemical Fluctuations Enables Simultaneous Optimization of Charge and Phonon Transport in BiTe Thermoelectrics
source: Angewandte Chemie International Edition
abstract: ABSTRACT BiTe‐based room‐temperature thermoelectric (TE) material family suffers from intrinsic efficiency‐limiting carrier‐mobility trade‐offs. Herein, we report an n‐type Bi 0.75 Sb 0.25 Te 0.7 S 0.15 Se 0.15 material with tailored local compositional fluctuations, which achieves a peak ZT of ∼ 0.64 at 377 K and a record‐high average ZT ave of ∼0.56 over 300–573 K, which stands as the maximum value for BiTe‐based TE systems. The excellent performance originates from conduction band flattening and dense intragranular dislocations, which are produced by the local compositional fluctuations. Band flattening spanning the Γ–A path together with enhanced valleys alignment increase the carrier effective mass, thereby improving the Seebeck coefficient. In addition, intragranular dislocations induce multiscale stress mismatches to achieve efficient phonon scattering, while reducing lattice elastic deformation and weakening phonon‐electron coupling. These synergistic effects allow this alloy a high power factor of ∼14.7 µW cm −1 K −2 and a low lattice thermal conductivity of 0.37 W m −1 K −1 at 377 K. This work proposes a feasible and effective strategy for modulating charge and phonon transport in TE materials.

title: Beyond Lithium Solvation: Tuning Cation‐Solvent‐Anion Interactions for Stable Lithium‐Metal Batteries
source: Angewandte Chemie International Edition
abstract: ABSTRACT Electrolyte chemistry in nonaqueous solvents is central to the electrochemical performance of high‐energy rechargeable batteries, yet the molecular basis of ion solvation in these systems remains incompletely understood. In conventional dipolar aprotic electrolytes, the high electron‐donating ability of the solvent favors cation‐dominated ion‐dipole interactions, such that anions remain largely free or are only weakly incorporated into cation solvation structures. Here we establish an explicit molecular picture of cation‐solvent‐anion ternary interactions in nonaqueous electrolytes and show that these interactions critically govern both bulk electrolyte properties and electrode‐electrolyte interfaces. We find that fluorinated ether‐based solvents, despite being widely regarded as non‐solvating diluents, can exhibit selective solvation of high‐electron‐donating anions, including halides and polysulfides. Coupling these ternary interactions to the redox chemistry of sulfur electrodes suppresses the dissolution and migration of polysulfide intermediates in ether‐based electrolytes, thus mitigating the shuttle effect and improving the cycling stability of Li°||S cells. More broadly, our findings revise the prevailing view of solvation in nonaqueous electrolytes and provide a molecular framework for solvent design and electrolyte formulation to advance high‐energy lithium‐ and other monovalent cation‐based rechargeable batteries.

title: Pathway Selection in Phenol Oxidation by a Ni(III)−Hydroxo Complex: Solvent and Substrate Control of Proton‐Coupled Electron Transfer
source: Angewandte Chemie International Edition
abstract: ABSTRACT Understanding the factors governing pathway selection in proton‐coupled electron transfer (PCET) remains a challenge in oxidative chemistry. Herein, we investigate phenol oxidation by a late‐transition metal hydroxo complex [Na(15c5)][Ni(PS3″)(OH)] ([Na(15c5)][ 1 ], 15c5 = 15−crown−5 ether and PS3″ = [P(C 6 H 3 ‐3‐Me 3 Si‐2‐S) 3 ] 3− ). Oxidation in CH 3 CN affords a mononuclear Ni(II) product, whereas reactions in THF generate a mixed‐valent Ni(II)Ni(III) dimer, revealing a solvent dependence of both reaction pathway and product distribution. Reactions in THF exhibit saturation kinetics and a kinetic isotope effect (KIE) value of 2.1, enabling direct interrogation of the elementary PCET step. Hammett, thermodynamic, and semiempirical free‐energy analyses independently reveal a substrate‐dependent mechanistic crossover: Electron‐rich phenols undergo concerted proton−electron transfer (CPET), whereas increasingly acidic substrates react through a stepwise proton‐transfer/electron‐transfer (PT/ET) pathway. In contrast, reactions in CH 3 CN display inverse KIE value together with anomalous free‐energy relationships, indicating a kinetically coupled regime in which precursor association and PCET become experimentally inseparable. Moreover, oxidation in CH 3 CN proceeds 10 3 −10 4 times faster than in THF, suggesting that the polar solvent facilitates PCET through stabilization of a polarized transition state. These findings establish an example of solvent‐ and substrate‐controlled pathway selection in PCET and highlight how the reaction medium can influence the mechanistic manifestation of O─H bond activation.

title: Entropy‐Triggered Mechanistic Reconfiguration: Unleashing Adjacent‐Site Oxygen Coupling to Circumvent Scaling Limit in Water Oxidation
source: Angewandte Chemie International Edition
abstract: ABSTRACT The oxygen evolution reaction (OER) remains the anodic bottleneck of water electrolysis for green hydrogen production. The conventional adsorbate evolution mechanism (AEM) is constrained by linear scaling relationships, whereas lattice oxygen involvement inevitably causes structural degradation, imposing a persistent activity‐stability trade‐off. Here, we realize a mechanistic transition from AEM to the oxide pathway mechanism (OPM), thereby circumventing the activity scaling limit, by constructing a noble‐metal‐free high‐entropy spinel oxide featuring a three‐dimensionally ordered macroporous (3DOM) hierarchical porous architecture. Mn/Al‐induced high‐entropy lattice contraction shortens adjacent‐metal distances, providing the geometric prerequisite for direct O–O coupling. Meanwhile, entropy‐driven electronic redistribution elevates Co valence and modulates Co–O covalency, optimizing oxygenated‐intermediate adsorption and enriching surface *OH species for subsequent O–O coupling. The 3DOM hierarchical porous framework further exposes OPM‐favorable sites and accelerates mass transport. Consequently, the catalyst delivers a low overpotential of 218 mV at 10 mA cm −2 , sustains stable operation for over 3000 h at 100 mA cm −2 , and enables an anion‐exchange membrane water electrolyzer to achieve 1.604 V at 1 A cm −2 with 2500 h durability. This mechanism‐guided high‐entropy design opens a route beyond the activity‐stability trade‐off.
