title: Fully integrated perovskite active polaritonic circuits
source: Nature
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Photonic integrated circuits are emerging as a key technology for compact, analogue and energy-efficient optical information processing
                    1
                    . Yet, their practical implementation remains limited by the intrinsically weak optical nonlinearities of conventional materials, which demand high power and large device footprints to achieve substantial nonlinear responses
                    2
                    . Exciton–polaritons, hybrid light–matter excitations of semiconducting materials, offer a promising route to overcome these limitations by combining strong optical nonlinearities with the high speed and scalability typical of photonic platforms
                    3–5
                    . However, despite their potential, fully integrated on-chip polaritonic systems simultaneously delivering room-temperature waveguide lasing, controllable optical routing and amplification have remained elusive. Here we demonstrate a fully integrated perovskite polaritonic circuit that brings these functionalities together in a single-step-grown platform. We realize precise and scalable polariton circuits with integrated gratings that act as both couplers and reflectors, enabling in-plane Fabry–Pérot cavities. These structures support robust in-plane polariton lasing with coherent guided emission at a geometry-defined wavelength, optical amplification of propagating polaritons and nonlinear optical phase control exceeding π, all within the same on-chip architecture. Our results establish perovskite polariton circuits as a scalable platform for active and interferometric integrated photonics.

title: Quantum resistance paradox of low-dimensional superfluids
source: Nature
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Resistance in standard conductors decreases with increasing cross-section. Yet, in low-dimensional superconductors and superfluids, residual resistance arises from topological fluctuations of the order parameter, manifesting as phase slips in one-dimensional (1D) and vortices in two-dimensional (2D) systems. How resistance and dissipation evolve as geometry interpolates between these regimes remains an open question. This evolution is masked in solid-state experiments by disorder, impurities and geometric imperfections
                    1–3
                    , and poses theoretical challenges due to competing dissipative processes and pronounced finite-size effects. Here, we use a defect-free unitary Fermi gas in a digitally programmable transport geometry to isolate geometric effects on superfluid dissipation and discover a paradox: in the crossover from one dimension to two dimensions, the resistance reaches a minimum. There, widening a channel increases its resistance. Narrower, quasi-1D channels show dissipation described by Langer–Ambegaokar–McCumber–Halperin theory of phase slips
                    4
                    . In this regime, varying the channel width yields the predicted exponential scaling of the activation factor over many orders of magnitude. Wider, quasi-2D channels show dissipation consistent with phase-slip events described by a finite-size vortex model
                    5
                    . The minimal dissipation in the dimensional crossover reflects a transition in the dominant dissipative mechanism, with both 1D and 2D events simultaneously suppressed. Our measurements suggest a route to minimizing dissipation in superconducting devices and provide a benchmark for theoretical efforts aimed at describing the dimensional crossover.

title: Optical Thin-Film Deposition on Bio-interfaces: Damage Mechanisms and Mitigation Strategies in PVD Environments
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The use of biological recognition elements in combination with high-performance optical thin films is the basis of next-generation bio-photonic devices; however, traditional physical vapor deposition (PVD) techniques can be detrimental to biomolecular activity. Here, we propose a cohesive physics-based model that views the damage to the bio-interface not through the lens of the deposition technique but as four fundamental energy-transfer modes: radiative (thermal evaporation), ionizing (electron-beam evaporation), kinetic (magnetron sputtering and high-power impulse magnetron sputtering, HiPIMS), and ablative (pulsed laser deposition). Each mode delivers energy in a unique way, such as thermal radiation, electronic excitation, momentum transfer, or impulsive ablation. This corresponds to different biological failure mechanisms, such as dehydration, radiolysis, mechanical denaturation, and stochastic thermal spikes. It is observed that the quality of the optical film and the survival of the biological component can be different: films with excellent macroscopic optical properties can hide the fact that the biological molecules at the interface have been severely damaged. We introduce a multi-parametric survival framework for designing bio-compatible thin-film fabrication strategies. This is achieved by incorporating literature-informed quantitative descriptions of hydration kinetics, mechanical stress evolution, and time-dependent energy accumulation. Device-level examples of plasmonic biosensors, integrated waveguide immunosensors, enzyme-based photonic chips, and lab-on-chip transducers demonstrate the ways in which damage due to different energy regimes affects the devices' sensitivity, stability, and operational lifetime. We pinpoint ways to construct bio-aware materials by implementing low-energy deposition ideas, adaptive plasma engineering, cryogenic processing, and machine-learning-assisted optimization. This regime-style paradigm evolves the bio-interface survival issue from an empirical constraint that is a mere afterthought into a predictive design parameter that can be deliberately used to co-fabricate biologically functional and optically pristine devices.

title: LRRK2-mediated phosphorylation of exocytic RABs disrupts neurotrophin/neuropeptide secretion
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Neuropeptide signals such as BDNF secreted from dense-core vesicles (DCVs) are essential for neuronal development, maturation and survival. RAB3 GTPases are established regulators of DCV exocytosis, but their functional diversity remains poorly understood. Here, we use live-cell imaging and neuropeptidomics to show that distinct exocytic RABs control DCV exocytosis in a neuron type specific manner, whereas RIM1/2 is a universal effector. Striatal neurons express both RAB3A and RAB27B but, surprisingly, only the latter controls DCV exocytosis. This is explained by selective phosphorylation of RAB3A by LRRK2, preventing its recruitment to DCVs. Finally, a LRRK2 hyperactive mutation associated with Parkinson’s disease disrupts DCV exocytosis in both hippocampal and striatal neurons. These findings uncover an unexpected diversity in controlling neuropeptide secretion in different neurons and establish LRRK2-mediated inhibition of RAB recruitment to DCVs as a powerful inhibitory principle that may also contribute to neurodegeneration upon gain-of-function mutations.

title: Distinct DNA-binding modes of Sp8 and Sp6 shape a hierarchical regulatory network in limb ectoderm
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Sp8 and Sp6 are closely related transcription factors expressed in the limb ectoderm, where they control proximo-distal and dorso-ventral patterning, yet their direct targets and molecular mechanisms have remained unclear. Combining genome-wide chromatin occupancy with transcriptomic profiling in vivo, we identify shared and specific targets and reconstruct the Sp8/Sp6 gene regulatory network, establishing Sp8 as its dominant, hierarchical node. Mechanistically, the two factors diverge: Sp8 binds DNA directly at canonical GC-rich Sp motifs, regulating targets including Fgf8 and Sp6 itself, whereas Sp6 acts as a transcriptional cofactor. Via indirect binding to AT-rich motifs through Dlx, both cooperatively regulate limb-patterning pathways, including Wnt, FGF, TGF-β/BMP, and Notch. Biochemical assays confirm that both form homo- and heterodimers and interact with Dlx5 through their zinc-finger domains. Together, these findings reveal how Sp8 and Sp6 orchestrate AER formation and dorso-ventral patterning, providing a mechanistic framework for congenital limb malformations such as split-hand/foot malformation.

title: A master gene for Drosophila male courtship prevents the behavior in females via a truncated protein
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Decades of studies have established that a terminal gene in the sex determination hierarchy, fruitless (fru), controls nearly all aspects of male courtship behaviors in Drosophila and many other insects. fru is transcribed in a sex-specific manner to produce male-specific Fru proteins (FruM) and was considered nonfunctional in females. In this study, we identify a female-specific truncated Fru protein (FruF) that is specifically expressed during the pupal stage and distributed in both cell bodies and neuronal projections, in contrast to FruM, which is expressed from larval to adult stages and localized to nuclei. We discover that FruF cooperates with another sex determination gene, doublesex (dsx), to prevent male-typical courtship in females. Knocking down fruF in dsx-expressing pC1 neurons induces courtship in females. These results reveal that the master gene for male courtship prevents this behavior in females via a truncated protein, thereby refining the canonical sex determination hierarchy that controls sexual development and behaviors.

title: Boosting Sensitivity of High-Dimensional Solid-State NMR of Proteins by Optimizing Coherence Transfers
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: TROP it or drop it: Owing to fast magic-angle spinning at frequencies above 50 kHz, solid-state nuclear magnetic resonance has evolved as a versatile method to decipher protein structure, dynamics, and chemical properties. While conceptually, higher-dimensional approaches such as 4D and 5D correlation spectra are capable of exceeding the established molecular-weight limitations by ameliorating signal overlap, their intrinsic implications for sensitivity and measurement times required have severely limited these important prospects in practice. Here we show that in high-dimensional experiments, the extensive use of dedicated transverse-mixing optimal control pulses (TROPs) can reduce the necessary measurement time by almost an order of magnitude. TROP’ed non-uniformly sampled experiments not only benefit from a multiplicative sensitivity enhancement in each complex time point due to concomitant transfer of both components of complex signals along multi-step magnetization transfer pathways, but additionally from facilitation of reconstruction with better raw data. Aided by the processing framework provided to future users here, the combination of an extensive use of TROPs with increased dimensionality hence presents itself as highly promising to ameliorate the conventional limitations of solid-state NMR.

title: Chromosomally unstable cancer cells exhibit heightened dependence on the mitotic SKA complex
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Aneuploidy and chromosomal instability are common characteristics of cancer but remain underexploited therapeutically. Chromosomally unstable cells are often selectively vulnerable to inhibition of the kinesin KIF18A, and this dependence is related to altered mitotic control. Here, we identify the spindle and kinetochore-associated (SKA) complex as a mitotic regulator that establishes a similar dependency. SKA complex loss is tolerated in cells with a defective mitotic checkpoint, but when mitosis is prolonged, it leads to mitotic errors and loss of viability. Genetic analysis reveals that the SKA complex and KIF18A are epistatic, although they function through mechanistically distinct mitotic pathways. SKA complex depletion selectively impacts chromosomally unstable cancer cells and mirrors the effects of KIF18A inhibition. We thus identify a cellular vulnerability associated with prolonged mitosis in chromosomally unstable cancers.

title: Selective mTOR inhibition via FLCN drives TFE3-dependent VLDL-TG secretion and protects from MAFLD/MASH
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Hepatic lipid homeostasis is controlled by multiple processes, including VLDL-TG secretion. We have previously shown that the FLCN/TFE3 branch of mTORC1 signaling controls hepatic fatty acid oxidation and de novo lipogenesis to protect mice from MAFLD. We now show that the FLCN/TFE3 pathway also controls VLDL-TG secretion via direct transcriptional activation of a broad program of genes involved in VLDL-TG secretion, including PCYT1A, the rate-limiting step of phosphatidylcholine synthesis. Loss of hepatic FLCN upregulates VLDL-TG secretion and prevents MAFLD, and this protection requires TFE3 and PCYT1A. The data unveil a new pathway that orchestrates multiple steps of VLDL-TG synthesis and secretion. The data also highlight that suppressing the selective FLCN/TFE3 branch of mTORC1 signaling maximizes hepatic lipid clearance by coordinately promoting fatty acid oxidation, suppressing de novo lipogenesis, and boosting VLDL-TG secretion, providing an attractive therapeutic target for the treatment of MAFLD.

title: N–Atom Transfer Reactivity of Terminal Cobalt Nitrides
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract We report the photogeneration and characterization of four-coordinate terminal cobalt nitrides (EmL)Co(N)(L) (L = pyridine, 4-dimethylaminopyridine) using a sterically encumbered dipyrrin ligand environment. The photolytic generation of the terminal nitride complexes were achieved in both the crystalline state and in frozen solution matrices to determine its molecular (single-crystal X-ray diffraction) and electronic structures (EPR). The solid-state structure, EPR spectrum, and computational analysis support a doublet ground state (S = 1/2) arising from antiferromagnetic coupling between high-spin CoII and a triplet nitride (3N–). Notably, the elongated Co–N bond distance (1.74(3) Å) suggests an attenuated π-interaction between the Co–N pair, consistent with the significant nitride-centered radical character. The electronic structure engenders unusual reactivity including (i) H2 cleavage, (ii) aromatic aryl ring expansion, and (iii) N–atom insertion into C(sp2)–C(sp2) bonds. The observed reactivity profile broadens our fundamental understanding of metal nitride chemistry as well as establishes a foundation for developing N–atom transfer reactions from formally high-valent metal nitrides.

title: Ikaros transcription factors prevent the activation of an endothelial cell program in bone marrow hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) are generally committed to the hematopoietic lineage, but how that commitment is maintained is not well understood. We show that the Ikaros family of transcription factors is essential for HSC identity. Ikaros, alone or in combination with Helios, is required to sustain the pool of multipotent HSCs and their downstream progenitor cells in adult animals, by directly repressing a core group of genes implicated in wound healing, cell junction organization, and actin cytoskeleton organization. Remarkably, upon in vivo or in vitro deletion of Ikaros or Ikaros+Helios, nearly one-third of the hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) rapidly exhibit an endothelial cell transcriptomic signature, and develop non-hematopoietic structures resembling CD144+ endothelial-like cells. These results indicate that adult HSPCs are highly plastic and prevented from activating an endothelial cell program by Ikaros family transcription factors.

title: TransA-MERFISH reveals divergent post-retinal direction-selective circuits
source: Nature
abstract: A major goal in neuroscience is to map the transformation of information as it flows through the brain. For example, neurons at many levels of the visual hierarchy are attuned to motion direction1-5. However, links between motion-selective computations and cell types at various stages of the visual hierarchy remain unidentified. A key first step in delineating these relationships is to map the wiring diagrams that connect different motion-selective cell types. Here we establish a systematic, cell-type-specific circuit-mapping method, combining an anterograde trans-neuronal fluorescent tracer (mWGA-mCherry)6 with spatial transcriptomics (multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridization (MERFISH))7,8 to establish TransA-MERFISH. We used TransA-MERFISH to comprehensively map the synaptic target cell types of four retinal ganglion cell subclasses in superior colliculus (SC) at cell-type resolution. These experiments unexpectedly revealed that retinal on-off direction-selective ganglion cells (ooDSGCs) innervate several direction-selective SC cell types, but do not innervate a SC cell type that was previously reported to display strong direction-selective responses. We validated these results using orthogonal approaches and demonstrated the sensitivity and specificity of TransA-MERFISH. Functional studies of SC activity before and after ablation of retinal direction-selective circuits confirmed that these computationally distinct, ooDSGC-dependent and -independent direction-selective cell types are commingled in SC. Together, our study establishes TransA-MERFISH as a robust framework for mapping wiring diagrams at the cell-type level and uncovers divergent computational mechanisms of motion detection in early visual processing.

title: Ultrastretchable Liquid-Metal Reinforced Polyelectrolyte Hydrogel Sensors for Multichannel Gesture Recognition and Robotic-Hand Control
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract With the development of wearable devices, human-motion monitoring, and human–machine interaction technologies, flexible sensing materials with high stretchability, rapid response, high sensitivity, and cyclic stability are increasingly required. To address conductive-pathway instability under large and repeated deformation, interfacial failure associated with layered liquid-metal/hydrogel architectures, and the difficulty in balancing mechanical deformability with sensing performance, this work reports a liquid-metal-reinforced polyelectrolyte hydrogel based on (2-(acryloyloxy)ethyl)trimethylammonium chloride (AETC) and eutectic gallium–indium (EGaIn) microdroplets. EGaIn was ultrasonically dispersed in water, introduced into an aqueous AETC precursor, and immobilized within the poly(AETC) network through UV-induced radical polymerization, yielding a bulk-dispersed AETC@LM hydrogel, where AETC@LM denotes an AETC-derived polyelectrolyte hydrogel containing dispersed EGaIn microdroplets. The effects of liquid-metal content on the morphology, chemical structure, mechanical properties, water retention, adhesion, and electromechanical sensing performance of the hydrogels were systematically investigated. Among the investigated formulations, LM200, prepared with 200 μL of the liquid-metal dispersion, exhibited the most favorable overall performance. It sustained a maximum tensile strain of approximately 3000% and provided strain sensing over 0–900%. Piecewise least-squares linear fitting of the strain response yielded gauge factors of 1.4 and 11.3 in the low- and high-strain regions, respectively. Similarly, piecewise least-squares linear fitting of the pressure response yielded sensitivities of 8.07 kPa–1 over approximately 0–7 kPa and 0.68 kPa–1 over approximately 8–25 kPa. LM200 retained approximately 95% of its initial mass after four weeks of ambient storage and exhibited adhesion to different substrates, with the highest adhesion strength observed on wood. The sensor showed response and recovery times of 0.24 and 0.18 s, respectively, and maintained repeatable resistance responses over 600 tensile cycles at 50% strain. Furthermore, five LM200 sensors were integrated into a five-channel smart glove. A ResNet50-based residual-learning model classified ten representative gestures from the acquired multichannel signals, which were also mapped to corresponding robotic-hand postures. The principal innovation of this work is the material-to-system integration of a bulk-dispersed liquid-metal/AETC polyelectrolyte architecture with strain–pressure dual-mode sensing and machine-learning-assisted multichannel gesture recognition. This integrated strategy establishes a structure–property–application relationship for liquid-metal-reinforced polyelectrolyte hydrogels and provides an experimental basis for large-deformation wearable sensing and intelligent human–machine interaction.

title: Redox-Active Self-Assembled Monolayers Drive Actuation in Hierarchical Nanoporous Gold
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Hierarchical nanoporous metals derived from dealloying offer lightweight, high-surface-area architectures with considerable promise for catalysis, energy storage, actuation, and sensing. Yet, the extent to which structural hierarchy and surface functionalization govern the functional properties of these materials remains largely unexplored. Here, we demonstrate reversible potential-induced actuation in millimeter-sized hierarchical nanoporous gold functionalized with ferrocene-terminated alkanethiol self-assembled monolayers (Fc-SAMs). In situ dilatometry in aqueous electrolyte reveals that redox conversion of the ferrocene headgroups generates pronounced mechanical deformation. Relative to a single-pore-size material, hierarchical nanoporous gold exhibits markedly larger strain amplitudes, consistent with its increased surface area and higher Fc-SAM coverage. Strikingly, the relationship between actuation strain and charge exhibits a quadratic dependence, in contrast to the linear behavior reported for earlier electrochemical actuators based on nanoporous gold. This finding highlights the significant role of the conformational dynamics of soft-matter SAMs in governing the mechanical response of metallic nanomaterials. In addition, the hierarchical material displays faster charging kinetics, supporting the notion that ion accessibility and mass transport are enhanced within the multiscale pore network. These results establish hierarchical nanoporous metals as a promising platform for chemo-mechanical sensing, in which chemical reactions at functionalized surfaces are directly transduced into measurable mechanical signals.

title: GTP hydrolysis by Ras proceeds without a stabilized nucleophilic water molecule
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: A comprehensive understanding of the Ras self-inactivation mechanism at atomic resolution—specifically, intrinsic GTP hydrolysis converting the GTP-bound active form to the GDP-bound inactive form—is essential for designing therapies against Ras-driven cancers. Conventional models describe a biphasic GTP-bound state: Ras interconverts between inactive state 1 and active, catalytically competent state 2. However, the structural pathway leading to Ras/GDP via these states remains unclear. Here, we use time-resolved serial femtosecond and synchrotron crystallography to capture GTP hydrolysis in Ras crystals loaded with photoactivatable caged GTP, across timescales from milliseconds to hours. Photolysis yielded Ras in state 1—a conformation lacking a stabilized nucleophilic water characteristic of state 2. Remarkably, this state persists for hours and converts directly to Ras/GDP without passing through state 2. These findings challenge the prevailing view that state 2 is essential and suggest that state 1 can directly support catalysis, offering an alternative conceptual basis for targeting clinically relevant Ras mutants that preferentially adopt this conformation.

title: A Ferrielectric Quasi-Racemic Crystal from an Enantiopolar Racemate
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Ferrielectrics, materials with partly switchable polarization, enable functional responses such as pyroelectricity and piezoelectricity. However, general design strategies for purely organic ferrielectric crystals remain scarce. Here we show that quasiracemates (QR), derived from enantiopolar centrosymmetric racemates, may provide a novel route to organic ferrielectrics. In these structures, quasi-enantiomers assemble into antiparallel polar columns that reveal the hidden polarization of the parent racemate. We hypothesized that a quasi-enantiomer bearing an acidic proton capable of forming an additional hydrogen bond could enable ferrielectric switching. Guided by this principle, we designed a QR composed of N-Ac-R-Val and N-Ac-S-Thr. The obtained crystals exhibit P21 symmetry and display ferrielectric characteristics, along with a large absolute pyroelectric coefficient (∼3.9 × 10–9 C/(K·cm2)) and a relatively low absolute piezoelectric response (d22 ∼ 2.27 pm/V). Deuteration of the acidic protons suppresses both the large pyroelectric response and the ferrielectric switching, providing strong evidence that these phenomena are driven by these protons and their local hydrogen-bonding environment. The macroscopic polarization and polar properties are further tunable by doping N-Ac-RS-Val with varying concentrations of N-Ac-S-Thr.

title: Toward a Deeper Understanding of Single-Atom Catalysis
source: Chemical Reviews: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Single-atom catalysts (SACs) promise control of heterogeneous reactivity at a molecular level by maximizing metal utilization and enabling deliberate tuning of local coordination and microenvironment. Yet SACs expose a central challenge in modern catalysis: the catalytically relevant site is often a working-state ensemble whose coordination, charge, spin state, adsorbate binding, and environment evolve under operating conditions. As the field expands toward bimetallic motifs, atom pairs, and hybrid SAC–nanoparticle architectures, multiple site families can coexist and interconvert. This complicates unambiguous site assignment and limits general structure–property relationships. This Review offers a critical mechanistic perspective on the use of single atoms in thermal catalysis, electrocatalysis, and photocatalysis. We first summarize stabilization strategies for host matrices, emphasizing how anchoring motifs and microenvironments govern site identity and its evolution. We then develop an evidence-based approach to site assignment that treats characterization as hypothesis testing and clarifies what can and cannot be concluded regarding coordination, electronic structure, site density, and working-state identity. Finally, we connect recurring descriptors to reactivity, selectivity, and durability. We thereby highlight benchmarking techniques, site-retention metrics, and durability protocols. The goals are reliable comparison of results across studies and the transition from empirical optimization to rational design of single-atom active sites.

title: Asymmetric NIR-II Voltage-Sensitive Dyes Enable Through-Skull Single-Cell Voltage Recordings of Neurons
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Optical measurements of neuronal membrane voltage in vivo are limited by light scattering at visible wavelengths. Fluorophores operating in the second near-infrared window (NIR-II) offer improved tissue penetration; however, the reported NIR-II dyes generally lack voltage sensitivity because their dynamic symmetric structures disfavor field-sensitive charge separation. Here, we report a chemically optimized family of asymmetric NIR-II voltage-sensitive dyes. The optimized probe shows 20% fluorescence changes per 100 mV and submillisecond response kinetics, together with membrane-associated fluorescence enhancement that suppresses the background. In combination with oblique NIR-II light-sheet microscopy, the probes enable through-skull recording of spontaneous and sensory-evoked neuronal spiking at single-cell resolution in the mouse cortex at depths of ∼200–300 μm in real time, resolving fast neural spike trains. These results establish an asymmetric NIR-II fluorophore design as a route for minimally invasive optical voltage imaging in vivo.

title: Flat-band-induced integer doping and phase transition in monolayer graphene
source: Nature
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    van der Waals heterostructures are stabilized by a delicate balance between van der Waals, elastic and Coulomb energies
                    1–4
                    . Because the interfaces are not covalently bonded, the constituent crystals can slide, rotate and reconstruct, resulting in several possible competing structural phases
                    2,5,6
                    . However, controlled tuning of this balance, and hence dynamical control over the stacking, has yet to be achieved. Here we report a dynamical heterostructure in which monolayer graphene is doubly aligned to bulk hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) and monolayer hexagonal boron nitride (mhBN) on either side. In such a system, a global structural phase transition, manifested as a change of crystalline symmetry observed by scanning tunnelling microscopy, could be induced by gating, magnetic field or temperature. This structural transition is accompanied by an exotic electronic transition: the doping of graphene switches between discrete levels, corresponding to an exact integer number of electrons or holes per moiré plaquette. We attribute this integer doping to charge trapping in localized, strain-induced pseudo-Landau levels (flat bands in reciprocal space
                    7–12
                    ), produced by moiré reconstruction (strongly enhanced by the mhBN). Electrical control of coupled structural and electronic phase transitions provides a route to engineering strain-induced flat bands and strain–Coulomb correlations in van der Waals heterostructures.

title: Humidity-Regulated MOF-Kirigami Passive Flyer
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract While passive flyers have gained increasing attention as an energy-efficient alternative to active unmanned aerial vehicles, they are challenged by limited flight time, high energy consumption, and large-scale deployment issues caused by heavy batteries and complex electronics. The dandelion seed, a natural passive flyer for wind-borne dispersal, has inspired the design of synthetic biomimetic counterparts that similarly leverage airflow for sustained locomotion. However, existing designs lack adaptive mechanisms to respond to diverse environmental conditions such as humidity variation, limiting their functionality in real-world atmospheres. Thus, a humidity-regulated passive flyer was presented here which integrates a ZPF-2-Co metal-organic framework (MOF)-polymer composite humidity actuator into a dandelion-seed-inspired kirigami structure. This flyer is capable of altering its flight position based on ambient humidity, enabling adaptive dispersal. A theoretical model about descent of a dandelion seed was established, using fluid dynamics simulations to analyze the flow field and pressure distribution. It is revealed that a vortex ring formed above the pappus increases drag and slows descent, while a restoring torque stabilizes the attitude and enables gliding upon tilt. Flight tests under seven humidity conditions reveal that the flyer descends vertically below 70% RH, transitions into stable gliding between 70% and 80% RH for controlled long-distance dispersal, and loses gliding stability due to flipping when RH exceeds 84.6%. The passive flyers developed in this work validate the humidity-regulating functionality of MOFs and their potential implementation in flexible devices, providing a foundation for future applications such as smart agriculture, distributed environmental sensing, and pollution tracking.

title: Competing capillary pathways govern buckling in drying porous microcapsules
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Capillary forces are fundamental in nature, lifting water in plants and supporting insects on ponds. Here, we show that capillary force can also buckle porous microcapsules as they dry. As water evaporates through the polymeric shell, an asymmetric air–polymer–water interface emerges and expands, where concave menisci at interfacial nanopores generate capillary (Laplace) pressure that deforms the shell. Optical imaging and accompanying phase-field modeling show that buckling initiates once the capillary pressure spreads over a critical surface area, then proceeds quasi-statically: Dimples nucleate, deepen, and ultimately evolve into a nested, double-shelled morphology, with each step rate-limited by water drainage through the porous shell. If the air–water front penetrates the microcapsule interior before buckling starts, the capillary loading area collapses and buckling is prevented. Drying therefore follows two competing capillary pathways: One drives buckling by sustaining distributed capillary loading on the shell, whereas the other suppresses buckling through early interior air invasion. Inspired by this insight, we preintroduce an internal air bubble into each microcapsule to act as a capillary sink and bias drying toward the air-invasion pathway. Our findings provide a mechanics-based blueprint guiding the design of robust, dry-stable microcapsules for pharmaceuticals, agriculture, and beyond.

title: Galectin-3 links microglial neuroinflammation to Aβ aggregation and lysosomal processing
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Neuroinflammation is a hallmark of Alzheimer’s disease (AD), yet the molecular mechanisms linking microglial dysfunction to amyloid-β (Aβ) pathology remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify galectin-3 (Gal3) as a regulator of plaque-associated microglial responses, linking Aβ aggregation, lysosomal function, and neuritic pathology. Using postmortem brain tissue from AD patients, we found that Gal3
                    +
                    microglia preferentially associate with cored plaques and correlate with increased LAMP1
                    +
                    dystrophic neurites. Gal3 was also detected in microglial lysosomal compartments, extramicroglial dystrophic structures, and in association with extracellular amyloid fibrils, suggesting roles in both intracellular and extracellular Aβ processing. In APP mice, Gal3 deficiency reduced plaque burden and neuritic dystrophy, increased plaque compaction, and enhanced TREM2 coverage around amyloid plaques. Mechanistically, in vitro microglial experiments showed that Gal3 modulates Aβ uptake and lysosomal processing, whereas lysosomal dysfunction promoted the accumulation of fibrillar Aβ from initially monomeric species, particularly in Gal3-deficient cells. Cell-free assays demonstrated that Gal3 preferentially binds fibrillar Aβ, inhibits secondary nucleation, and alters fibril morphology, while Gal3-modified fibrillar Aβ reduces N2a neuronal cell number. Finally, in silico structural analyses identified candidate Gal3 interactors enriched in leucine-rich-repeat and immunoglobulin-like proteins, supporting a role for this lectin in immune receptor regulation. Complementary in vivo transcriptomic profiling showed that Gal3 deletion suppresses type I interferon and microglial neurodegenerative transcriptional signatures. Together, these findings position Gal3 at the interface between Aβ remodeling, lysosomal homeostasis, and plaque-associated microglial responses in AD.

title: Structural basis for the selective inhibition of the PI3KC3-C2 complex by Rubicon in endolysosome maturation and mitophagy
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Rubicon is a negative regulator of autophagy and the endolysosomal network (ELN) and an antagonist of the class III phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase complex II (PI3KC3-C2). Inhibition of Rubicon is considered a potential means to therapeutically upregulate autophagy and the ELN to treat Parkinson’s disease and other conditions characterized by autophagic and ELN dysfunction. Rubicon is specific for the UV radiation resistance-associated gene protein (UVRAG)-containing PI3KC3-C2 over the purely autophagic ATG14-containing PI3KC3-C1 complex. Here, we determined the high-resolution cryoelectron microscopy structure of PI3KC3-C2 in complex with the PI3KC3-binding domain of Rubicon and compared it to cryo-EM structures of unbound PI3KC3-C2 and PI3KC3-C1. Rubicon binds directly to PI3KC3-C2 only via the BARA domain of the BECN1 subunit, which is common to both C1 and C2. The selectivity of Rubicon for the PI3KC3-C2 complex over the PI3KC3-C1 complex is attributed to a conformation of the BECN1
                    BARA
                    domain induced by UVRAG, rather than to direct contact with UVRAG or direct antagonism by the ATG14 subunit of PI3KC3-C1. Targeted disruption of the Rubicon:PI3K3-C2 structural interface by site-directed mutations enhances mitophagic activity in human epithelial cells to levels comparable to those observed in Rubicon knockout cells. Similarly, disruption of the interaction in Rubicon-overexpressing hippocampal neurons restored lysosomal flux to wild-type levels. These data show that suppressing the function of PI3K3-C2 can fully account for the negative regulatory effects of Rubicon in the autophagy and ELN pathways.

title: ACSS2 modulates endothelial glycolysis in angiogenesis
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Endothelial cells (ECs) sustain high glycolytic flux and display remarkable metabolic plasticity. Although molecular pathways regulating endothelial glycolysis are well characterized, metabolic mechanisms underlying hypoxia-induced glycolytic activation during angiogenesis remain poorly understood. Here, we show that acetyl-CoA synthetase 2 (ACSS2) serves as a critical metabolic modulator, coupling acetate utilization with glycolytic flux to control EC function and angiogenesis. The high level of ACSS2-mediated acetate-to-acetyl-CoA conversion in angiogenic front ECs sustains acetyl-CoA levels, which are essential for EC proliferation and retinal vascularization. Conversely, endothelial-specific
                    Acss2
                    deletion disrupts pathological angiogenesis and normalizes tumor vasculature. Mechanistically, ACSS2 maintains hypoxia-inducible factor 1α transcriptional activity and stabilizes glucose transporter 1, thereby preserving glycolysis. Pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase 4 knockdown rescues metabolic and functional defects in ACSS2-deficient ECs, revealing the vital role of acetyl-CoA homeostasis in modulating hypoxic endothelial metabolism. Taken together, these data establish ACSS2 as a pivotal regulator of vascular development and suggest that targeting acetate metabolism may be an effective way to modulate pathological angiogenesis.

title: Bionic skin with hair follicle regeneration capability from acoustic fluids-mediated 3D printing
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Tissue engineering holds substantial potential for constructing normal skin with appendages such as hair follicles, directly restoring skin’s complete physiological functions. The current challenge lies in recreating biomimetic hair follicle organs with high-level cell density and architecture. Here, we developed an acoustofluidic-assisted 3D bioprinting platform to fabricate bionic skins with efficient hair follicle regeneration capability. Pre-formed hair follicle germs, derived from co-cultured epidermal and dermal mesenchymal stem cells, were encapsulated within a hydrogel bioink. Controlled acoustic fields generated flow vortices that directed cell migration and promoted organized cellular assembly from initially disordered states. Guided cell aggregates were then patterned through bioprinting to construct a grid-structured bionic skin. This architecture provided stable 3D support while maintaining high porosity, enabling efficient gas exchange. The printed bionic skin exhibited well-organized spatial cell distribution, high cellular viability, and promising differentiation potential. Further in vivo experiments demonstrated the efficiency of the bionic skin in accelerating mature hair regeneration, showing promise for clinical alopecia treatment.

title: An ensemble of functionally distinct factors enables spatial quality control during proteasome base assembly
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: The proteasome is an essential mediator of the ubiquitin–proteasome system and a complex molecular machine. Hallmarks of de novo proteasome assembly include dedicated chaperones and many subunits, culminating into major assembly intermediates such as the base. Emerging evidence suggests that proteasome assembly is subject to extensive quality control (QC). To understand mechanisms of QC, we examined a crucial assembly checkpoint during base assembly. Our findings reveal sequential mechanisms of QC, in which a checkpoint complex is first assembled, then sequestered into the nucleus, away from ongoing proteasome assembly in the cytoplasm. Assembly of this checkpoint complex depends on noncanonical ubiquitination of the Nas2 chaperone. The Nas2 ubiquitin chain functions as a scaffold by binding the Rpn13 ubiquitin receptor, which is distantly positioned within the same complex. Rpn13 also positions the ubiquitin chain to its neighboring Hul5 ubiquitin ligase, for continual chain elongation to further stabilize this complex. Ubiquitin-mediated assembly enables spatial sequestration of this checkpoint complex through its intrinsic nuclear localization signal (NLS). This NLS on Rpt4 specifically targets this checkpoint complex into the nucleus, emphasizing the importance of spatial compartmentalization. Our findings reveal that proteasome assembly integrates multiple functionally distinct components as QC factors (1 assembly chaperone, 2 ubiquitin regulators, and 1 NLS) to distinguish correct vs. incorrect assembly events en route to a proteasome holoenzyme. These components are not simply passengers in assembly intermediates with their activities reserved for mature proteasomes, but their fundamental functions in cellular proteolysis may begin by first ensuring the accuracy of proteasome assembly.

title: Neuronal IL-34 programs microglial activity via the TGF-β–MEF2C axis to constrain neuroinflammation following brain ischemia
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Brain ischemia induces robust neuroinflammation driven by microglial activation, yet whether ischemic neurons actively reprogram microglial phenotypes to limit inflammation remains elusive. Here, we identify neuronal interleukin-34 (IL-34) as a critical immunomodulatory signal that maintains microglial homeostasis after cerebral ischemia. We demonstrate that ischemic injury augments IL-34-CSF1R signaling between neurons and microglia. Neuron-specific overexpression of
                    Il34
                    (Syn1-
                    Il34
                    tg
                    mice) attenuated infarct volume and neurodeficits after middle cerebral artery occlusion, whereas neuronal
                    Il34
                    knockdown exacerbated brain injury. Microglial depletion abolished IL-34-mediated neuroprotection, suggesting microglia as essential effectors. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed that neuronal IL-34 preserved homeostatic microglial signatures (
                    P2ry12, Cx3cr1, Tgfbr1
                    ), while suppressing inflammatory activities (
                    Il1b, Tnf, Cxcl2
                    ) through upregulation of the transcription factor MEF2C. Mechanistically, IL-34 activated TGF-β signaling in microglia and inhibition of TGF-β signaling abolished the protective effects of IL-34, whereas microglia-specific
                    Mef2c
                    overexpression rescued neuroprotection despite TGF-β blockade. Thus, ischemic neurons deploy IL-34 to orchestrate the immunoregulatory activity of microglia via the TGF-β–MEF2C axis, representing a previously unrecognized endogenous mechanism counteracting neuroinflammation. Our study reveals neuronal IL-34 as a potential therapeutic target for ischemic stroke.

title: Sleep pressure is increased by protein fragments and decreased by processive proteolysis
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Sleep is universal among animals, yet the molecular-level causes and functions of sleep are incompletely understood. The fragment generation hypothesis (FGH) posits that sleep, at least in part, is an adaptive response to protein fragments, many of them protein-sized, that accumulate during wakefulness owing to cleavages by proteases, including caspases and Ca
                    2+
                    -activated calpains. According to the FGH, these fragments are a source of homeostatic sleep pressure that increases during wakefulness, and one function of sleep is to decrease protein fragment levels through their slower production and faster degradation during sleep. Predictions of the FGH have not previously been tested. Using zebrafish, we show that pharmacological inhibition of caspases decreases sleep, in agreement with the prediction of the FGH that a slower production of protein fragments would decrease sleep pressure. Pharmacological inhibition of the proteasome is shown to have the opposite effect, an increased sleep, in agreement with another prediction of the FGH, that sleep pressure would increase if fragments are protected from their proteasome-mediated degradation. Consistent with this prediction, a caspase-generated subunit of the activated caspase-3 is strongly upregulated by a sleep-increasing inhibition of the proteasome. The increase of sleep by proteasome inhibitors was found to be reduced by inhibition of calpains, suggesting that calpain-generated, proteasome-degradable protein fragments contribute to sleep pressure. Pharmacological inhibition of calpains also causes a decrease in rebound sleep after sleep deprivation, as predicted by the FGH. Together, these results suggest that the FGH may provide a molecular-level explanation of a cause and function of sleep.

title: Dynein-dependent positioning of multiple organelles regulates adaptive gene expression during oxidative stress
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Cells respond to environmental insults through well-characterized changes to their transcriptome and proteome. The contribution that reorganization of intracellular architecture makes to the adaptive stress response is much less understood. Here, we reveal a conserved spatial response to oxidative stress in which the microtubule motor dynein enhances perinuclear clustering of multiple membrane-bound organelles. These events are triggered by reactive oxygen species and protein kinase C and occur without increased association of dynein with its activator dynactin, pointing to a noncanonical mechanism for stimulating retrograde transport. Using a chemically inducible system for dispersing individual organelles, we show that perinuclear localization of multiple compartments potentiates oxidative stress–induced gene expression, with distinct genes depending on inputs from either combinations of organelles or individual compartments. Together, these findings implicate positioning of multiple membrane-bound compartments in gene expression regulation and identify coordinated organelle trafficking by dynein as an additional regulatory layer in the cellular stress response.

title: Local influenza forecasts outperform state-level forecasts in the United States
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Accurate outbreak forecasts are critical for timely and effective public health response. In the United States, however, most forecasts are produced at the state level, which can mask substantial substate heterogeneity and limit their utility for local planning. We generated and evaluated forecasts of the percentage of Emergency Department visits attributable to influenza across 173 large metropolitan Health Service Areas (HSAs) using a gradient boosting quantile regression model and compared their accuracy to forecasts derived from state-level data alone. At a 1-wk, 2-wk, and 3-wk horizon, local forecasts outperformed state-based forecasts in 98.8%, 90.8%, and 78.6% of HSAs, respectively, achieving mean weighted interval scores that were on average a 39.2% lower (95% range: 5.9 to 76.7%), 19.6% lower (−6.3 to 59.5%), and 11.4% lower (−11.7 to 44.9%), respectively. The performance advantage of local forecasting was strongest in HSAs representing a smaller share of their state’s population and increased with the proportion of the HSA population living in urban areas and the number of metropolitan areas within a state. These results, based on an analysis of HSAs with populations greater than 250,000, demonstrate that fine-scale modeling can substantially improve forecast accuracy and highlight the potential value of local forecasts for outbreak preparedness and response.

title: Tunable spectral correlations of highly multimode visible light via broadband quantum frequency conversion
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Multimode squeezed states of light are a resource for achieving quantum advantage in computing and sensing, where spatial or temporal modes have been the experimental norm. In our experiments, we generated highly frequency-multimode infrared quantum light and showed how adiabatic frequency conversion can be used to convert the quantum state to visible wavelengths while concurrently manipulating the joint spectrum by realizing a configurable many-port frequency-domain beamsplitter unitary transformation. We report near-unity efficiency quantum frequency conversion over a bandwidth >45 terahertz, which allowed us to measure the state with an electron-multiplying CCD (EMCCD) camera-based spectrometer, at noncryogenic temperatures. The parametric amplification and conversion of >400 frequency modes yielded an overall mean of ∼700 visible photons per shot and photon statistics consistent with squeezing. Our work shows how many-mode quantum states of light can be generated, manipulated, and measured with efficient use of hardware resources, motivating the use of frequency encoding in quantum optics.

title: Curvature-guided chiral collective organization of myoblast tissues
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Surface curvature is a fundamental geometric cue in tissue morphogenesis, yet its role in guiding collective cell organization has remained elusive. Here, we show that curvature acts as a geometric control parameter that shapes supracellular alignment and chirality while modulating myogenic differentiation in myoblast tissues. Cells cultured on curved substrates self-organize into robust helical assemblies whose handedness is set, and can be reversed, by the sign of curvature: convex fibers produce right-handed helices, whereas concave channels invert the chirality. We identify a clockwise bias in single-cell motion associated with the helical actin cytoskeleton. A minimal continuum theory coupling an effective chiral drive to curvature quantitatively captures the emergence and reversal of tissue-scale chiral alignment. On substrates with spatially varying curvature, local curvature gradients organize patterned multicellular architectures while preserving a global handedness. Curvature is also associated with myogenic state, with higher curvature linked to reduced or delayed differentiation. Together, these findings reveal how complex geometries shape the alignment, symmetry, and cellular state of living tissues.

title: Four phases and temporal threshold of population calcium response during locomotion in cortical astrocytes
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Calcium activity is a major form of astrocyte excitability. Astrocytic calcium events arise spontaneously and in response to behavior, but how unitary events shape population-level activity remains unclear. Using two-photon imaging in the primary somatosensory cortex of awake mice running on a freely rotating disk, we analyzed calcium dynamics during quiescence and locomotion. During quiescence, population fluctuations were driven mainly by the co-occurrence of new events rather than by their enlargement. During locomotion, responses progressed through four phases: emergence of new events, their merging into a superevent, fragmentation, and an afterburst. These responses combined the progressive recruitment of active regions with amplification of a reproducible spatial calcium pattern. New events emerged within the first seconds after locomotion onset, indicating a rapid astrocytic response. A full population response required about 5 s of locomotion: Shorter episodes failed to develop the superevent and produced markedly smaller responses. In suprathreshold episodes, the superevent displayed a reproducible ΔF/F pattern. Hotspots within this pattern had shorter latencies and were also more active during quiescence. A dynamic mode decomposition with control model driven by synthetic or real locomotion inputs reproduced the response phases, temporal threshold, and superevent pattern. These findings show that locomotion-evoked astrocytic calcium activity is an ordered, threshold-dependent population process with reproducible spatiotemporal structure that can be approximated by a low-dimensional dynamical system.

title: Paul R. Ehrlich: Visionary pioneer and public scientist for nature and humanity
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Paul R. Ehrlich is legendary for his scientific insight and impact—and even more so for bringing science to the public through writing, speaking, and, most famously, twenty-some appearances on the Tonight Show Starring Johnny Carson. He was quick-witted—he would readily add quick-tempered, with chagrin—and could bring down a house. Paul cherished deep friendships and nature. He loved collaborating with his wife of 71 years, Anne H. Ehrlich, and with innumerable students and colleagues all over the world. He made transformative contributions of astonishing range, including in ecology and evolution, biodiversity and conservation, human population and overconsumption, and the integration of ecology and economics. He was deeply committed to racial and social justice, reflected in his actions and writing.

title: A periplasmic regulator establishes adaptive impermeability to control carbapenem entry
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Outer-membrane permeability is a major determinant of antibiotic susceptibility in Gram-negative bacteria and is generally thought to be controlled through transcriptional regulation of porin expression. Here we identify the small periplasmic protein PtrA as a regulator of OprD-dependent carbapenem permeability in
                    Pseudomonas aeruginosa
                    . PtrA promotes imipenem resistance without altering OprD abundance, associates with OprD-containing membrane complexes and reduces intracellular imipenem entry. Using zinc and copper as complementary physiological signals, we show that PtrA-mediated permeability control is mechanistically distinct from CzcRS-dependent repression of
                    oprD
                    and precedes transcriptional porin depletion. These findings define a two-phase mechanism in which rapid periplasmic regulation provides an immediate adaptive response before transcriptional remodeling of the outer membrane. Our work identifies adaptive impermeability as a previously unrecognized mechanism linking environmental sensing to dynamic control of bacterial outer-membrane permeability.

title: Anthropocentric comparisons with human language impede our understanding of whale communication
